10024-beneath-the-banner-being-narrative:
F. J. Cross's Beneath the Banner, in its second edition of 1895, gathers narratives of noble lives and brave deeds. Its motto comes from Gordon: I have done my best for the honour of our country. Its subtitle promises stories of men and women steady when under fire.

Among them are Only a Nurse Girl, the story of Alice Ayres, and a slave trade warrior. There are also stories of Sir Samuel Baker, who served in Ceylon and, in 1869, at the Khedive's request in Egypt. Cross writes for young readers, with illustrations. The book offers heroism as example, in short, stirring tales.
10102-the-czar-s-spy-the-mystery-of-a-si:
Chevalier William Le Queux's 1905 spy romance, subtitled The Mystery of a Silent Love, opens in His Britannic Majesty's service. Chapters ask why a safe was opened, visit a house over the water, and watch the mystery increase through confidences and gathering clouds.

A surprise, life's counter-claim, and strange disclosures follow, in Le Queux's popular manner of secret service and romance. The silent love of the title runs beneath the espionage, giving the intrigue a human heart. Readers get an Edwardian spy tale, brisk, romantic, and full of hidden doors.
10112-american-political-ideas-viewed-fr:
John Fiske gave these three lectures at the Royal Institution in London in May 1880, then published them as a short book. He asks how American politics fits into the long story of human government, from early village assemblies to the federal union. His answer is evolution, not sudden invention: institutions grow and change over time.

Fiske traces town meetings back to old Aryan councils and shows federalism as a later stage of that same growth. He compares American practice with older states to show what is new and what is inherited. Readers get a clear, Victorian-era case for reading United States history as part of world history.
10342-the-velvet-glove:
Henry Seton Merriman, whose real name was Hugh Stowell Scott, wrote this Spanish romance of love, revenge, and honor. Its hero, Marcos, moves through walled towns, cloisters, inns, and quarries, where old wrongs still burn. The velvet glove of the title hides an iron hand, as later chapters make plain.

A royal adventure, a pilgrimage, and a stormy petrel of a heroine named Juanita carry the plot toward war's alarm and a casting vote. Cousins, monks, and makers of history cross Marcos at every turn. Readers get a rich, old-style tale of Spain, told with color, pace, and high feeling.
10397-affairs-of-state-being-an-account-:
Burton E. Stevenson published this adventure novel in 1906, subtitled an account of surprising adventures that befell an American family in the land of windmills. The land is Holland, where windmills, canals, and old towns frame a tale of princes, skeletons, and bold plans. Stevenson, author of mystery novels, writes with pace and humor.

An American family meets distinguished arrivals at Weet-sur-Mer, a rescue, and a crooked path through Tellier's schemes and Pelletan's skeleton. A prince gains an ally, and night events push the plot on. Readers get a bright, old-style romance of travel, intrigue, and American pluck abroad.
10444-the-peace-negotiations-a-personal-:
Robert Lansing, who served as United States Secretary of State, wrote this personal narrative of the Paris peace talks after the First World War. Lansing explains why he wrote: to record President Wilson's presence at the conference and the making of the League of Nations covenant. The book is both memoir and argument.

Chapters treat Wilson's plan, Cecil's rival plan, self-determination, mandates, secret diplomacy, the Shantung settlement, and the Bullitt affair. Lansing notes where American plans were lacking and where talks broke down. Readers get a sharp, insider account of how the 1919 peace was shaped and strained.
122-the-return-of-the-native:
Egdon Heath broods over a village where love and ambition collide. Thomas Hardy's Return of the Native opens with Eustacia Vye, who dreams of Paris and escape. Clym Yeobright returns from Paris hoping to teach, while Thomasin and Diggory Venn circle them.

Six books trace marriages, quarrels, and a mother's pride toward tragedy on the heath. Eustacia's longing, Clym's ideals, and Wildeve's charm pull the plot toward ruin. Hardy makes the heath itself a character, vast and indifferent. The novel ranks among his greatest tragedies. Hardy's heath scenes, from bonfires to storms, give the tragedy its brooding power.
12789-ladies-must-live:
Alice Duer Miller's 1917 novel Ladies Must Live opens at a New Year's house party, where the most fashionable people in New York gather in the country. Mrs. Ussher's guests trade wit, flirtation, and hard judgments about money, marriage, and reputation. Illustrations by Paul Meylan mark key scenes, from a hand dried finger by finger to a lover's declaration.

Beneath the comedy runs a serious question: how are women without fortunes to live decently in a world that prices them by marriage? Miller's heroines scheme, work, and love with clear eyes. The novel blends social satire with sympathy for women making their own way.
12887-laugh-and-live:
Douglas Fairbanks wrote Laugh and Live in 1917 as a cheerful creed for young Americans, illustrated with scenes from his films. Chapters urge readers to whistle and hoe, take stock of themselves, profit by experience, build personality, and keep clean in body and mind. Honesty, democracy, good reading, and seizing chances recur as themes.

Fairbanks argues that filth of mind and body sinks a person fastest, while successful people live in the open, exercise morning and evening, and meet life with sure aim. A close-up of the actor closes the book. The volume charms as a star's sunny self-help sermon from the silent-film age.
12912-the-price-of-love:
Arnold Bennett's 1914 tale The Price of Love opens in old Mrs. Maldon's sitting room, where Rachel Louisa Fleckring wears an immense blue pinafore apron. The apron shields her frock in the kitchen, slips off in a second, and turns a drudge into a boudoir figure, yet on Rachel it only adds a piquant air. She is a downright girl, scorning pretence.

Money drives the plot: nine hundred and sixty-five pounds vanish from the house, and Thomas Batchgrew rages, since he himself left the sum there and lost a good investment. Theft theories, a cinema visit, runaway horses, and a changed man follow, with Rachel and Mr. Horrocleave at the close. Bennett counts love's cost in cash, pride, and patience.
13396-sweetapple-cove:
George Van Schaick's 1914 novel opens in John Grant's diary, as a city doctor leaves Hudson laboratories and great hospitals on a sudden whim. He settles in a little house in Sweetapple Cove, among people whose accent sounds unfamiliar to the outside world, in two best rooms rented so cheaply he feels ashamed.

Grant fishes for trout, fries them over a fire with a pan fitted to a long stick, and carries heavy loads of meat back from the hunt. A woman's instinct to mother a wreck of manhood brought in from the sea softens the rough coastal life. The book follows a healer who sought change and found it in work, weather, and the plain kindness of a fishing village.
13499-two-little-savages-being-the-adven:
Ernest Thompson Seton writes and illustrates the adventures of two boys who live as Indians and learn woodland life. Yan and Glenyan build a shanty, dam a pond, and study the marsh, woods, and animals around them. Over three hundred drawings show how each camp, trap, and sign is made.

A neighbour refuses seasoning timber for a barn sill or gate posts, but spares two logs and sends a team, warning the boys not to steal more. Yan sketches a hemlock trunk while watching, not for love of sketching but to pass the time and learn the tree. Seton teaches nature through play: tracking, building, and living outdoors, with the patience of a naturalist behind the boys' games.
13881-the-case-of-mrs-clive:
Catherine Clive published The Case of Mrs. Clive in 1744 to defend actors against theatre managers. The Augustan Reprint Society reissued it with an introduction by Richard C. Frushell. Clive asks what happens when only two theatres are allowed and their masters league together. Actors, she argues, must then take whatever salary or treatment managers offer.

The pamphlet speaks for performers' rights in Georgian London. Clive writes with solid sense and sprightly wit, as a verse tribute notes. Her case blends personal grievance with public principle. Theatre historians value it as an early labour protest from the stage. The reprint makes a rare tract easy to read today.
14521-memories-a-story-of-german-love:
Max Müller's Memories, a story of German love, reached English readers in George P. Upton's 1902 Chicago translation. Müller, the Oxford philologist, wrote the original as Deutsche Liebe, and Upton warns that its elegant simplicity is hard to carry across.

The memories follow a narrator's love for a noble young woman, recalled in scenes of music, painting, and talk, including an Italian painter who copies a Paris picture for her. The prose is gentle and reflective, more meditation than plot. The book offers a quiet, idealizing romance, prized by readers who loved Müller's scholarship and sentiment.
14543-false-friends-and-the-sailor-s-res:
This slim 1884 volume pairs two moral tales for young readers, False Friends and The Sailor's Resolve, with illustrations of domestic scenes. Lady Grange and her son Philip open the first tale.

Philip falls in with two men his mother distrusts, and his conduct distresses the household until illness and repentance bring a reckoning. The second tale follows a sailor's firm choice in temptation. The stories preach loyalty, obedience, and steadfastness in plain Victorian style, with prayers and proverbs framing each lesson. Parents of the era bought such volumes for Sunday reading.
14784-timid-hare-the-little-captive:
Mary H. Wade's 1916 story for children follows Timid Hare, a little captive among Native American people of the plains. Captured, brought before the chief and settled in a new home, the child faces hard work, change and a visit that tests courage.

A mischief maker, a happy day, a dog feast and a festival follow, with moving day, a journey, a medicine man and a winter hunt. Colour plates show Buffalo Rib as a handsome youth, Black Bull hurrying home and the medicine man watched with wonder. Wade, author of the Little Cousin series, writes sympathetically and simply, though her period terms now need care. The tale is adventure told at a child's pace.
1481-a-daughter-of-eve:
Balzac's novel of Parisian marriage follows two Maries, friends from the provinces, whose fates divide in the capital. One marries for love and struggles; the other marries for rank and learns the price of a fashionable life, where debts, lovers, and salon talk threaten a household's peace.

Through balls, letters, and quiet confessions, Balzac shows how society tests a wife's loyalty and a husband's pride. The title points to Eve's daughters and their common trials. It is a keen, sympathetic study of marriage, money, and the small choices that decide a woman's life.
15242-desert-love:
Joan Conquest's 1920 romance, in three parts called Seed, Flower, and Fruit, opens with Jill gazing eastward over a crowd in flowing robes. Women in black burkas and veils sit below her, men in turbans and tarbooshes stand around, and Jill's golden hair and blue eyes mark her as an outsider. The desert setting drives the tale.

Love, danger, and Eastern color carry Jill through a story of passion and choice, in the popular romantic style of its day. Conquest, author of Leonie of the Jungle, writes lushly and fast. Modern readers will find the novel dated in its views, but vivid as a sample of 1920s desert romance.
15415-tramping-on-life-an-autobiographic:
Harry Kemp published this autobiographical narrative in 1922, through Boni and Liveright, in a Garden City edition that ran to twelve printings by 1927. Kemp dedicates the good in the book to his wife, Mary Pyne, and opens with his grandmother's tales: he never knew his mother, who died of the family weakness after bearing him. He was born in the early eighties in Youngstown, Ohio.

The narrative follows a poor boyhood, with a country doctor uncle riding in free from Antonville to tend a sick aunt, and a child who teased until he was switched. Kemp writes as a tramp poet in the making, moving from muddy streets and family stories toward the road. The book's pull lies in its plain, vivid memory: a working-class American childhood told without polish, in the voice of one who lived it.
15454-imperium-in-imperio-a-study-of-the:
Sutton E. Griggs published this novel in 1899, framed as papers handed over by Berl Trout, late Secretary of State of the Imperium in Imperio. Trout, the preface says, knew every detail of that great organization from its founding to his death. He was a warm friend of Bernard and Belton, the two young men at the story's heart. The frame gives the tale a documentary air.

Chapters follow Belton from a small beginning through school, a parson's advice, a young rebel's turn, love and politics, and marriage. Later chapters cross the Rubicon, weigh weighty matters, and part ways, as a secret Black government debates its answer to white supremacy. Griggs wrote one of the earliest Black nationalist novels, bold in its premise and earnest in its argument about race, power, and the future.
15472-emblems-of-love:
Lascelles Abercrombie published this poetic work, designed in several discourses, with a hymn to love opening the volume. The hymn pictures love as a deep thought, with human lives as its speech, spoken and burned through by imagining. A dedication to his wife closes the book, and an epilogue bears that dedication's name.

Three parts carry the design: discovery and prophecy, with Vashti; imperfection, with three girls in love named Mary, Jean, and Katrina; and virginity and perfection, with Judith and The Eternal Wedding. A marriage song follows. Abercrombie treats love as a spiritual emblem, not a mere romance, in verse and prose discourses that ask what love reveals about human nature. The work suits readers of early modernist poetry.
15989-the-fatal-glove:
A novel by Clara Augusta, author of The Rugg Documents, issued in 1892. A short story, Constitutionally Bashful, by an unidentified author, follows the novel in this file. The Fatal Glove opens in New York rain, where Arch Trevlyn, a little street-sweeper, earns pennies and half-dimes. Sunshine gilds Saint John's tower as his day turns.

A glove, lost or found, draws Arch into a mystery of love and fortune. Augusta writes with brisk, popular skill, mixing street life with romance. Business, rain, and mud give way to hope. The novel delights as a period melodrama: a poor boy, a fatal token, and a fate that turns on a glove.
16037-great-epochs-in-american-history-v:
The first volume of Great Epochs in American History, described by famous writers from Columbus to Wilson, edited by Francis W. Halsey. Funk and Wagnalls issued the ten-volume illustrated set, copyrighted 1912 and 1916. Halsey, associate editor of The World's Famous Orations, adds introductions and notes to each piece. Volume one covers voyages of discovery and early explorations, 1000 to 1682.

Famous writers retell Norse voyages, Columbus, and the first explorers of American coasts. Halsey's notes join the pieces into a continuous story. The tone stays stirring and patriotic. The volume serves young historians well: America's beginning, told by the writers who made it vivid.
16094-for-woman-s-love:
Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth's 1890 novel opens on a striking rise in life. Regulas Rothsay, once a barefoot foundry boy doing odd jobs, has just been elected governor of his state by a record vote. He is thirty-two, engaged to the finest young lady in the country, and set to marry one day and take office the next. Foundry foreman Silas Marwig tells the tale with pride.

From that bright start, Southworth spins a popular romance of love, ambition, and the claims of the past on a new-made man. Her plots are busy, her villains plain, and her heroines warm-hearted, in the style that made her a best-selling author. Readers who enjoy Victorian melodrama will find this a lively, old-style love story.
16156-then-marched-the-brave:
Harriet T. Comstock's 1904 story for young readers opens when the king's men held sway and mystery and plot ruled a small American town. Andy McNeal, a boy in a little house near the troubles, meets a stranger in the night. He is crowned in jest and slips through a cave. Then strange talk leads him to headquarters. Chapters titled Then Marched the Brave and Peace point to a Revolutionary tale.

Illustrations show Andy at the oars, in female attire, and facing a general, with Janie and Burr among the cast. Comstock, author of Molly, the Drummer Boy, writes lively history adventure for children. The book offers young readers courage, disguise, and the thrill of living through a nation's fight for freedom.
16356-brannon-s-picture-of-the-isle-of-w:
George Brannon, an artist who lived forty years on the Isle of Wight, wrote this guide for visitors who had only two or three days to tour the island. It opens with climate, geology, and local history, then leads the traveler through Newport, Cowes, Ryde, and the romantic southeast coast, from Shanklin Chine to Ventnor and beyond.

Brannon pairs practical routes with notes on castles, villages, and coastal views, with pictures to match. The book is brisk and helpful, aimed at the hurried tourist rather than the scholar. It still works as a window on Victorian seaside travel, when the Isle of Wight was a favored short holiday.
1684-the-egoist-a-comedy-in-narrative:
George Meredith sets this comedy of manners at Patterne Hall, where Sir Willoughby Patterne, handsome, rich, and entirely pleased with himself, expects the world to admire him on his own terms. His engagement to Clara Middleton, and his earlier tie to Laetitia Dale, give the plot its two women and its slow unravelling.

Meredith works through dialogue and close looks at motive, showing how Willoughby's ego turns every kindness into a claim. Clara's quiet revolt against a match she cannot love drives the book. Its comedy comes from watching a man who calls himself devoted learn, too late, how little he has listened.
17083-adventures-of-a-sixpence-in-guerns:
A native of Guernsey tells this 1857 tale through a bright new sixpence handed out on New Year's Day. Two little girls take the coins to town with their mother, and the coin's path carries the reader through shops, streets, and island life. The opening scenes stress sun, dew, and neat crowds, not the cold and want of an English winter.

The charm lies in small sums and small choices: what a sixpence can buy, who handles it next, and what each owner hopes for. Written for young readers, the book mixes a gentle moral with a homely tour of the island. It still works as a sweet, old-style story about money, luck, and kind use.
1718-manalive:
A great wind brings Innocent Smith to Beacon House, and with him come strange luggage, a banner, and a habit of breaking rules for reasons no one can guess. His housemates watch him climb roofs, wave banners, and court danger, and half of them suspect him of murder, burglary, and worse.

The second half of the book answers every charge, one by one, and the answers reframe Smith's wild acts as a deliberate celebration of ordinary life. Chesterton's point is that habit dulls wonder, and Smith's antics are meant to wake his friends up. It is a comic defence of joy, argued through farce and finished with a trial.
17200-angel-agnes-the-heroine-of-the-yel:
Wesley Bradshaw's 1873 pamphlet tells the sad, romantic history of Agnes Arnold, adopted daughter of Samuel Arnold. Wealthy, lovely, and engaged to wed, Agnes went to nurse yellow fever patients at Shreveport, Louisiana, and labored three weeks without rest. Her intended husband, who followed her there, died before her, and the two were buried side by side.

Bradshaw calls her Angel Agnes and frames her death as a hope of blessed life beyond, with terrible plague scenes beside the love story. The pamphlet mixes news, sentiment, and moral praise in the style of its day. Readers of epidemic history will find a moving, if florid, tribute to a young nurse's sacrifice.
17500-the-return-of-the-native:
Thomas Hardy's novel, in this 1912 edition, takes place on Egdon Heath, the brooding stretch of Dorset heathland that shapes everyone who lives on it. Clym Yeobright, the native of the title, comes back from Paris with plans to teach his neighbours. His hopes tangle with Eustacia Vye, who longs for a grander life, and with Thomasin, Wildeve, and the reddleman Diggory Venn. The book is divided into sections with names like The Three Women and The Fascination.

Hardy writes the heath itself as a force, almost a character, pressing on love, marriage, and ambition. Misunderstandings, secret meetings, and stubborn pride drive the story toward tragedy. Readers get one of Hardy's great Wessex novels, praised for its landscape writing and its unsparing view of people who want more than their place allows.
17699-the-evolution-of-love:
Emil Lucka wrote this study of the evolution of love, translated by Ellie Schleussner and first published in Great Britain in 1922 by George Allen and Unwin. The book is built in stages. The first stage treats the sexual instinct. The second stage treats love itself, opening with the birth of Europe.

Chapters then cover the deification of woman as a first form of metaphysical eroticism, through the love of the troubadours, the Queen of Heaven, and Dante and Goethe, to Michelangelo. Readers get a philosophical history of love in European culture, learned and speculative. The book suits readers of cultural history and of the philosophy of love.
17751-direct-legislation-by-the-citizens:
J. W. Sullivan wrote this 1893 book to argue that citizens should make laws themselves, through the initiative and the referendum. He was the second in a line of small books on just rule, and he looks to Switzerland as the chief model.

Chapters describe Swiss votes, Swiss public care, and the Swiss commonwealth, then turn to direct law-making in the United States. Sullivan holds that a peaceful vote can do what revolt once did, and he pleads for tools that let the people check their rulers. It is a short, keen tract, still apt for debates on direct democracy.
17875-the-american-prejudice-against-col:
William G. Allen wrote The American Prejudice Against Color in London in 1853, calling himself a refugee from American despotism. Allen, a Black professor, had fled the United States after a mob rose against his marriage, and he tells the tale to wake British readers.

Chapters run from personalities and servility to the mob, dark days, and a brightening close, with a short personal narrative of his own. A letter from Congressman Gerrit Smith praises Allen's worth and mind. The book is a bold, early protest against American racism, written in exile and still sharp today.
18086-a-dozen-ways-of-love:
L. Dougall wrote A Dozen Ways of Love in 1897, printed in London by Adam and Charles Black, and dedicated to M. S. E., without whose aid the books would never have been written. Dougall, author of Beggars All and The Zeit-Geist, here gives twelve tales of love in its many forms.

Tales run from young love and a marriage made in heaven to thrift, a taint in the blood, a commercial traveler, witchcraft, and a pauper's golden day. The book opens with a curate walking grey cliffs with Violetta, the vicar's daughter. Dougall writes with a keen, moral eye. It is a thoughtful, Victorian story book on love's dozen faces.
18440-logic-deductive-and-inductive:
Carveth Read, author of The Metaphysics of Nature and Natural and Social Morals, wrote this textbook of logic, deductive and inductive. The fourth edition, enlarged and partly rewritten, appeared in London from Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent and Company, after a first edition in 1898 and reprints through 1920. Read writes for students who need logic as a working tool.

Early chapters define logic, treat proof in general, divide the subject, and set out its uses and its relations to mathematics, concrete sciences, metaphysics, and psychology. A second chapter analyzes propositions: subject, predicate, and copula, compound propositions, and the import of propositions. Readers get a clear, systematic logic: how arguments are built, tested, and judged, in plain academic prose.
1851-the-woman-in-the-alcove:
Anna Katharine Green's Woman in the Alcove opens with a woman wearing a diamond and gloves, and a set of explanations that do not quite fit. It follows Anson Durand through arrest, suspense, and a night voice that changes the case. The narrator, astonished by the inspector and astonishing him in turn, pieces the crime together from broken china and small domestic facts.

Green builds the mystery from household detail rather than from grand deduction. The alcove of the title — a room within a room — gives the book its central image: a murder seen sideways, by someone who was not meant to see it. It is a strong example of Green's careful, humane detective work.
18665-molly-make-believe:
Eleanor Hallowell Abbott's novel, issued at New York in 1911 with the Century Company after a 1910 copyright, carries pictures by Walter Tittle. It opens on a dark, cold city morning with Carl Stanton bedridden, rheumatism clawing at his back, a stale glass of water and half a grapefruit beside him. In his swollen fingers rustles a crisp letter from Cornelia, who has gone south for the winter.

Cornelia refuses daily letter writing, dislikes love letters, and says one avowal of love should suffice, while Stanton fumes at her coolness. The title points to the make-believe game that follows between them. Abbott writes with wit and warmth about courtship at a distance.
18951-benefits-forgot-a-story-of-lincoln:
Honoré Willsie's 1917 story Benefits Forgot: A Story of Lincoln and Mother Love follows a southern Ohio family through church life, war, and a meeting with Abraham Lincoln. The tale opens at a donation party, where church members debate how much sugar and molasses a growing twelve-year-old boy, Jason, should be allowed for the year. They weigh generosity against scarcity with comic seriousness.

Later chapters follow a circuit rider, the coming of war, and finally Mr. Lincoln himself, as Jason and his mother endure the hardships and loyalties of a border community in wartime. Willsie frames the story as one of mother love, showing a mother who gives, sacrifices, and is in turn remembered or forgotten by those she serves. The novella blends domestic humor, Civil War history, and sentiment into a tribute to maternal devotion in an age of national crisis.
19134-the-empire-of-love:
W. J. Dawson wrote this 1907 religious book on love as the ruling force of Christian life. He dedicates it to a woman who, in his words, practised its teachings in compassionate work for others in London. Love, he argues, feels no burden and seeks to redeem lives most lost to hope.

Dawson urges readers to meet Jesus first-hand in the Gospels, not through codes built by teachers who lost the spirit in rules. He contrasts Pharisee law-making with the simple, novel life of Christ. Readers get an earnest devotional work on faith lived as love, not as mere rule keeping.
19335-oscar-the-detective-or-dudie-dunne:
Old Sleuth wrote this fast-paced detective tale, issued in New York in the late eighteen hundreds. Its hero, Dudie Dunne, poses as a foppish dude on city streets, then drops the mask to chase criminals with speed and nerve. The opening trick, played on a gang of street toughs, sets the tone for the whole book.

Later scenes test Dunne's honor as well as his skill, when a client asks him to prove guilt or innocence without favor. The story is a period piece of dime-novel detection: disguise, chase, and a detective who insists on fair play even when a case turns personal.
19346-new-word-analysis-or-school-etymol:
William Swinton wrote this 1879 school book, New Word-Analysis, on the etymology of English derivative words, with exercises in spelling, analysis, definition, synonyms, and use. It remodels his 1871 Word-Analysis, keeping old methods and adding much new practice matter for pupils. Swinton won a gold medal for textbooks at Paris in 1878.

Lessons define prefix and suffix with plain cases such as unsafe, remove, and circumnavigate, then set long exercises on primitive and derivative words, from grace and sign to steamboat and trustworthy. Readers get a thorough Victorian word study, still useful for spelling and word roots.
19658-the-judgment-of-eve:
May Sinclair was a British novelist known for sharp studies of women's inner lives. Her 1907 novel The Judgment of Eve opens in a small social world with clear ranks. Aggie Purcell of the Laurels is, by common consent, the prettiest young lady there. She is also the best dressed and best mannered. The other young ladies must settle for her leavings.

Sinclair used such small-town stages to test pride, desire, and judgment. A heroine measured by looks and manners invites a fall. The title hints at Eve, the first woman judged for wanting more. Sinclair later became a noted voice in modern fiction. This early novel shows her eye for social pressure already at work.
20134-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-at-:
Laura Lee Hope published Bunny Brown and His Sister Sue at Christmas Tree Cove in 1920. Sue dances on the grass and begs for one more ride. A board on a sawhorse makes a fine seesaw in the yard. She races to it, keen to tip up and down once more.

Christmas Tree Cove gives the Brown children a new place to roam. Seaside air, trees, and small tasks fill their days there. Each Bunny Brown book keeps peril low and cheer high throughout. Young readers get safe adventure, sibling fun, and lessons in kindness and care.
20165-the-theory-and-practice-of-perspec:
G. A. Storey wrote The Theory and Practice of Perspective, a guide for artists. Storey was a painter and a member of the Royal Academy. He turns, in one passage, to air and light in a scene. Two figures in the same dress must differ in tone by distance.

Mountains, too, grow less distinct as air thickens between viewer and peak. Such rules help a flat canvas show true depth and space. Storey writes for working artists, not just students of theory. Readers get clear, tested craft advice from a painter who taught it for years.
20476-hymns-for-christian-devotion-espec:
Hymns for Christian Devotion was prepared for Universalist congregations, whose faith stressed God's love for all. The book gathers hymns for public worship across the church year. Its editors drew on older collections and on new writing.

The preface is frank about its borrowings. A few hymns came from a copy of the new Cambridge Unitarian hymn book, handed to the editors in sheets. For those pieces it was not known whether they were original or not. They appear here among many whose sources were sure. Hymnals like this one shaped what American congregations sang each Sunday.
20484-real-life-in-london-volumes-i-and-:
Pierce Egan's Real Life in London, issued in two volumes, follows the rambles and adventures of two young men about town. Bob Tallyho and his cousin Tom Dashall sample the city's high life and low life. Egan's earlier Life in London had made such tours famous.

The fun runs on sport, wit, and wine. One song praises coming home triumphant at night with the spoil, like roisterers shouting and gay. With a bottle and song, the singers refresh themselves and defy dull wisdom. The book preserves Regency slang, taverns, race meetings, and street scenes in rich detail.
20715-marriage-and-love:
Emma Goldman's essay Marriage and Love attacks the wedding institution root and branch. Goldman, the anarchist writer and lecturer, argued that marriage as practiced was an economic bargain, not a union of love. She first published the essay in her book Anarchism and Other Essays.

Marriage is primarily an economic arrangement, she writes, an insurance pact. It differs from the ordinary life insurance agreement only in that it is more binding and more exacting. Its returns are insignificantly small compared with the investments. Goldman demanded that love be freed from law, church, and money, and the essay still stings.
20726-a-slave-is-a-slave:
Space fleets, ranked officers, and strict orders fill the opening of A Slave Is a Slave. Line-Commodore Vann Shatrak wears black battle dress with gold marks of rank. His bald head and sharp face mark him as a hard man in a hard service.

Beneath the space-war surface, the title states the book's hard theme in plain words. A man held as property stays a slave, whatever fine words others use. The story uses a future empire to test old questions about power, rank, and human worth. It suits readers who like bold science fiction with a moral sting.
20997-the-nu-rnberg-stove:
An old schloss turned guard-house, with gold heraldic work, houses the Nurnberg stove's tale. A stone man-at-arms stands life-size in his niche, dated 1530, Louisa de la Rame notes. Battlements and frescoes set the German scene in rich, old colour.

Ouida, as de la Rame was famed, tells of a boy who hides in a great stove. August's love for the huge, fair stove drives this tender tale. Art, poverty, and a king's whim cross in its pages. The Nurnberg Stove ranks among her best-loved tales for the young, grave and glowing by turns.
21261-the-attempted-assassination-of-ex-:
On October 14, 1912, John Flammang Schrank shot ex-president Theodore Roosevelt in Milwaukee as Roosevelt campaigned to return to the White House. Oliver E. Remey, Henry F. Cochems, and Wheeler P. Bloodgood compiled this account the same year for the Progressive Publishing Company of Milwaukee. Illustrations show the shirts Roosevelt wore and a page of his speech manuscript.

The bullet lodged in Roosevelt's chest, slowed by that manuscript, and he famously spoke before seeking care. Schrank was judged a paranoiac by five alienists and sent to the hospital at Oshkosh. The editors dedicate the narrative to Roosevelt as the greatest American of his time.
21496-problems-of-immanence-studies-crit:
J. Warschauer argues against a loose view of God's presence in Problems of Immanence, published in 1909. His studies, called critical and constructive, take aim at theosophy and kindred systems. A line from Colossians, in Moffatt's rendering, stands as the book's watchword.

Warschauer holds that if God is simply all things, evil must come from God's own will. Or else evil shrinks to a mere seeming, a kind of non-being. He finds both results fatal to faith and to conduct. The chapters trace how errors in thought flow into errors in religion and life.
22155-the-expressman-and-the-detective:
Allan Pinkerton, founder of the famous detective agency, published The Expressman and the Detective in 1874. Pinkerton swore his stories were true to life. His preface, signed from Chicago in October 1874, warns that the incidents may seem marvellous. Truth, he answers with the old adage, is stranger than fiction.

The tale follows an express company's money, a trusted messenger, and the detective sent to test him. Pinkerton's men work by disguise, patience, and shadowing across cities. The book launched a whole series of Pinkerton detective volumes. They taught American readers to see the detective as a professional, and they remain primary evidence of how Pinkerton wanted his agency remembered.
22404-the-story-of-the-white-rock-cove:
The Story of the White Rock Cove is a tale set on a bright coast. Its path starts from a garden and passes through a shrubbery. A little wire gate leads into a natural wood beyond.

The wood clothes the upper part of a hillside there. The path descends rapidly, steep in places, through the trees. It emerges now and then for clear, wide views. Below lies beautiful Braycombe Bay, dancing and sparkling in sunshine. That sparkling morning opens a story tied to its cove. Readers get seaside scenery rendered with real affection. The place itself becomes a character before events unfold.
23146-and-all-the-earth-a-grave:
A budget shocks a bureaucrat in And All the Earth a Grave. An official staggers into his office at the new year and drops, dazed, into his chair. His department's budget, he learns, stands at a hundred times the expected figure. That works out to fifty times what he requested.

Money multiplied beyond reason is the first symptom in this tale of a world pricing its own end. The title promises a grave as wide as the Earth, and the story works toward it through ledgers rather than explosions. Its method is satire with a chill, clerks and budgets carrying apocalypse in triplicate. Readers who like their doom administered by memorandum will find this a neat, cold specimen.
23197-subversive:
Subversive is a work of science fiction built around a smooth sales pitch. Warren Dickens leans forward and runs through a routine he has plainly given many times. He asks Coty a pointed question about everyday buying: what do you really purchase when a shop takes a small card charge for a bar of soap?

The setting is an ultra-market, a store far more advanced than an ordinary shop. Dickens's pitch treats a tiny fee on a common item as a window into a whole system. Readers get a future-world tale where money, cards, and commerce carry the hidden weight of the plot.
2347-the-adventure-of-the-dying-detectiv:
Holmes appears to be dying of a rare Asian disease in The Adventure of the Dying Detective, and only Watson's devotion keeps him at the bedside. Arthur Conan Doyle turns the sickroom into a trap: the supposed invalid is acting, waiting for his enemy to confess to a murder. The story's suspense lies in Watson's ignorance and Holmes's performance.

The reveal, when it comes, is pure Holmes: the disease was a ruse, the culprit caught by his own gloating. It is among the most theatrical of the short stories. Fans will relish its twist.
23574-socialism-positive-and-negative:
Robert Rives La Monte wrote this nineteen hundred seven book on socialism, positive and negative, printed in Chicago by Charles H. Kerr. An Isaiah motto on man made more precious than fine gold opens the book. Chapters take up science and socialism, the material view of history, the law of surplus value, and the class struggle.

Marxism and ethics, a note instead of a footnote, the nihilism of socialism, the biogenetic law, and kismet follow, with an early piece from the International Socialist Review of September nineteen hundred. La Monte writes as a socialist thinker testing his own creed, praising its science while probing its morals. Readers of political history will find a frank, period argument, useful for seeing how American socialists debated their faith a century ago.
23733-incidents-of-the-war-humorous-path:
Alf Burnett, comic delineator and army correspondent, published Incidents of the War in Cincinnati in 1863. A sketch of the author by Enos B. Reed opens the book, praising Burnett as a fellow of infinite jest who always looked on the bright side of life.

The sketches, letters, and anecdotes that follow mix humor, pathos, and description from Civil War camp and field. Burnett set tables roaring with quaint sayings and a keen eye for the grotesque. For modern readers, the book is a soldier-humorist's view of the war as it was being fought, in the very year of Gettysburg.
23789-cruel-as-the-grave:
Mrs. Emma D. E. N. Southworth published Cruel as the Grave in 1888, one of her many melodramatic novels of love, jealousy, and fate. Its epigraphs come from Medea: a woman who gave her heart forsakes her lover for another, and burns at her nature's planted stake.

Chapters introduce the Berners of the burning hearts, John Lyon Howe, and Sybil Berners, with a beautiful stranger and a landlord's story. Down in the dark vale, at Black Hall, and in the guest-chambers, a jealous bride's story unfolds through love and jealousy to a chapter titled Cruel as the Grave. Southworth's readers will find her in full, passionate form.
23846-the-flag-replaced-on-sumter-a-pers:
William A. Spicer read The Flag Replaced on Sumter before the Rhode Island Soldiers and Sailors Historical Society in February 1884, and it was printed at Providence in 1885. Spicer's narrative begins with Lincoln's election in November 1860 and the South's predetermined plan of secession.

By February 1861, seven slave states had formed the Southern Confederacy under Jefferson Davis at Montgomery. On Inauguration Day, the United States flag flew at only three points south of Washington: Fort Sumter, Fort Pickens, and Key West. Spicer follows South Carolina's ordinance of December 20, 1860, and Major Robert Anderson's stand at Sumter, toward the day the flag returned.
24672-the-god-of-love:
Justin Huntly McCarthy wrote this romance, published at New York and London in 1909 by Harper and Brothers. Its epigraph, from Chaucer, praises love as a mighty lord. Chapters open with a May-day queen, a child and a child, and Vittoria, whose words and warnings drive the plot.

McCarthy, author of If I Were King, sets his tale in a world of lovers, poets, and quarrels, where love rules like a lord. His heroine Monna Vittoria sends messages and sounds warnings, and lovers and lasses follow their hearts. Readers get a graceful, romantic novel, rich in colour and old-world charm.
24882-privateering-and-piracy-in-the-col:
John Franklin Jameson edited this volume of documents on privateering and piracy in colonial America, published by Macmillan in 1923 under the Colonial Dames of America. The papers, in English, Dutch, French, and other tongues of the 1600s and 1700s, show how colonies licensed sea raiders and then tried to hang them.

Early sections cover Providence Island. Later notes follow Captain Kidd and the pirate Bradish, seized with his wealth at Block Island, broken out of prison, and sent to England with Kidd in 1700. Jameson's notes tie each paper to its source. The book gives historians the raw stuff of sea robbery, in the words of those who ordered, chased, and tried it.
24889-the-greater-love:
Chaplain George T. McCarthy of the United States Army published The Greater Love in Chicago in 1920, his memoir of service in the World War. The chapters follow him from home through Camp Dodge, Camp Mills, and the Leviathan at sea to Brest, billets in France, and the front at Puvinelle, Thiacourt, and Rembercourt.

McCarthy tells of an old school turned hospital under Doctor Thiery, whose soldier son fell at St. Quentin, and of Army doctors joining its staff to save lives. His frontispiece shows him before the attack at Rembercourt. The book closes with Armistice Day and the road home, a chaplain's plain record of love made inventive and skillful under fire.
25001-an-old-man-s-love:
Anthony Trollope's An Old Man's Love, published by William Blackwood and Sons in 1884 in two volumes, is, as his son Henry notes, the last of his father's novels completed. The Landleaguers was written after it but never fully finished. The story turns on Mr. Whittlestaff, Mary Lawrie, and John Gordon, with Mrs. Baggett, the Reverend Montagu Blake, and Croker's Hall among the fixtures. Mary accepts Whittlestaff, and Gordon's returns unsettle every arrangement.

Whittlestaff's dinners, journeys, and meditations pace the second volume, from Little Alresford to the Green Park and back to Croker's Hall. One passage shows him resolving, as he walks across country, to let the man's coming pass as a misfortune. He trusts that time would eventually erase him from memory, while leaving the two lovers alone in his own parlour. The novel is Trollope at his most quietly observant.
25117-with-the-naval-brigade-in-natal-18: Lieutenant Burne's With the Naval Brigade in Natal, published in London in 1902, is known here only from its front matter. The text supplied holds the title page, dedication, contents, and illustration list, with no journal narrative. Its contents promise service under General Sir Redvers Buller during the relief of Ladysmith, with chapters on Colenso, Spion Kop, and naval guns in action. Appendices on gunnery, equipment, and despatches are also listed.
25291-theism-or-atheism-the-great-altern:
Chapman Cohen's Theism or Atheism, published by the Pioneer Press in 1921, is a freethought argument against belief in God. Cohen, a leading British secularist, examines theism first, then defends atheism as the honest alternative.

Part one asks what God is, where the idea came from, and whether humans possess a religious sense. It tests arguments from existence, causation, and design, and points to nature's disharmonies, evolution, and pain. Part two answers charges about prejudice, morals, and agnosticism, citing vestigial structures such as the appendix and wisdom teeth as evidence against design.
26519-to-love:
Margaret Peterson's 1917 novel takes its title from Stevenson's line that to love is the great amulet which makes the world a garden. It follows Joan Rutherford, twenty-three, living on her own in London. Her only people, an old uncle and aunt in the country, disapprove of her independence. Joan, childlike in looks but obstinate of chin and frank of eye, has kept her rooms for six months.

Gilbert Stanning laughs uneasily that Joan does not believe in marriage and he cannot afford to marry, suggesting they are the right sort to drift together. Joan's attic near King's Road, Chelsea, with sloping roofs and a tiny window, becomes her refuge and her testing ground. The novel traces love, pride, and independence among young Londoners of its day.
27257-electricity-for-the-farm-light-hea:
Frederick Irving Anderson's Electricity for the Farm, published by Macmillan in April 1915, teaches light, heat, and power by inexpensive methods from the water wheel or farm engine. Even the tiny trout brook becomes a thing of utility as well as joy, in the Fitz Water Wheel Company's illustration.

Part One covers water power, with chapters on magnets and wire: wind cotton thread on a spool, connect it to a dry battery, and add an iron core to concentrate the magnetism. Anderson, author of The Farmer of To-Morrow, writes a practical handbook for farms beyond the power lines.
27606-the-library-of-william-congreve:
John C. Hodges of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, reconstructed the library of William Congreve. The New York Public Library published it in 1955, reprinted with additional illustrations from its Bulletin of 1954 and 1955. A frontispiece shows the first page of Congreve's Bibliotheca, with entries partly obliterated by the first hand.

When Congreve died in 1729, his friend and publisher Jacob Tonson called his collection genteel and well chosen, and urged his nephew to buy it. Congreve had willed the books to Henrietta, the young Duchess of Marlborough, who kept them intact for her youngest daughter Mary. Mary's 1740 marriage to the fourth Duke of Leeds sent the books to Hornby Castle in Yorkshire, where most remained until about 1930.
27856-bandit-love:
Juanita Savage, author of The City of Desire and Passion Island, published Bandit Love in 1931 with the Dial Press by arrangement, reprinted by A. L. Burt Company. The novel opens on Rotten Row on a brilliant June morning during the London season, at the week of the International Horse Show.

Miss Myra Rostrevor rides a high-spirited bay that rears and bucks before the retired colonels of the liver brigade, while a mounted policeman grins, knowing she can handle almost any horse. Romantic and dashing, the book promises love, adventure, and a heroine who rides her own course.
27894-the-pearl-of-lima-a-story-of-true-:
Anne T. Wilbur translated this story of true love from the French of Jules Verne, as it appeared in Graham's American Monthly Magazine in April 1853 under the title The Pearl of Lima. The tale opens on the Plaza-Mayor of Lima at evening, as promenaders fill the streets in the cool air.

Chapters follow a Spanish grandee, the hatred of the Indians, a betrothal, conquerors and conquered, and the cataracts of the Madeira. Early Verne, romantic rather than scientific, the story shows the young writer's feeling for South America before his famous voyages extraordinaires.
28084-malcolm-sage-detective:
Herbert George Jenkins wrote Malcolm Sage, Detective as a set of linked cases around a quiet English investigator. Sage, aided by Department Z and Sir John Dene, takes on cattle maiming in Surrey, a stolen Admiralty memorandum, a garage outrage, and a marmalade clue. Lady Dene's breakfast-table teasing opens the book with humour.

Each chapter gives Sage a fresh puzzle, solved by close watching and clear deduction rather than force. Jenkins keeps the tone light, with comic servants and society folk around the crimes. Readers who enjoy classic British detective stories will find Sage a calm, likeable hero.
28229-anderson-crow-detective:
George Barr McCutcheon wrote Anderson Crow, Detective in 1920, copyright 1918 to 1920, as a comic detective novel. Anderson Crow, town marshal, faces a night to be remembered, a veiled lady and a shadow, a vicious Lucius, and a candidate for marshal who stirs the town. John T. McCutcheon drew the pictures, including youngsters grabbing Crow's ear.

Chapters follow Jake Miller's hanging scare, shades of the Garden of Eden, and a surrender shouted in the street. McCutcheon, author of Brewster's Millions, keeps the tone light and small-town. Readers get a gentle parody of detective fiction, with a marshal more lucky than brilliant.
28264-cleek-the-master-detective:
T. W. Hanshew's Cleek, the Master Detective, Garden City, 1918, collects twelve cases of Hamilton Cleek, a detective once on the other side of the law. Gordon Grant drew the pictures. Cleek, charming and quick with disguise, takes on riddles of a red crawl, a sacred son, a caliph's daughter, and a ninth finger.

Other cases treat a wizard's belt, a lion's smile, a steel room, Siva stones, and a rainbow pearl. Hanshew, author of Cleek of Scotland Yard, keeps the puzzles fair and the pace brisk. Readers of classic detective fiction get a hero who knows thieves because he once was one.
28274-the-beauties-of-nature-and-the-won:
Sir John Lubbock wrote The Beauties of Nature and the Wonders of the World We Live In, New York and London, 1892, as a popular survey of natural beauty and science. Lubbock moves from scenery, seasons, and the aurora to animal life, plant life, woods, fields, and mountains, with notes on ants, flowers, trees, and the sleep of plants. A beech group at Burnham fronts the book.

His aim is to show that love of nature brings happiness, and that small creatures matter as much as great ones. Lubbock writes in clear, gentle prose for general readers. The book remains a charming Victorian introduction to natural history.
28621-the-metamorphoses-of-publius-ovidu:
J. J. Howard's translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses into English blank verse, volume 1, was printed in London in 1807 for the author. Howard dedicates the attempt to William, Earl of Lonsdale, hoping to render Ovid's beauties more accessible to English readers. He also aims to chasten the prurience of Ovid's ideas and language, fitting the work for general perusal.

The first book opens with chaos, where earth, sea, and sky lie undistinguished in one dead form. A world lord then dissolves the strife, placing firm earth apart from blue sky and rolling back the waves. Readers get Ovid's changes of shape in measured verse, from creation onward.
2915-a-bit-o-love:
John Galsworthy's A Bit o' Love plays out on Ascension Day in a village of the west of England, among the Strangway family and their neighbors. Michael and Beatrice Strangway, Mrs. Bradmere, Jim Bere, Jack Cremer, and the Burlacombe, Trustaford, and Jarland families fill the cast. Scenes move from Strangway's rooms to the village inn, the church, and Burlacombe's barn.

Gossip drives the action, as Mrs. Bradmere probes for scandal and the innkeeper Godleigh answers with a house rule against scandal-mongering. The play tests forgiveness against village judgment, with love offered in small measures rather than grand gestures. It shows Galsworthy's village manner, where reputation matters as much as fact.
29471-the-velvet-glove:
Harry Harrison's science tale treats a near future where robots, above all specialist robots who do not know their place, have a rough time. True, a Robot Equality Act existed on paper, but so what? In New York, a bad town for robots that year, Jon Venex fits a key into a hotel room door, having paid extra for the largest room in the house. He dares not complain or seek his money back.

Venex sighs with relief as the door swings open on a room fully three feet by five feet, with more than enough room to work in. Harrison's irony is plain: equality on paper means little without room to live. Fans of Harrison will enjoy a sharp, funny fable on rights, robots, and the velvet glove of power.
29721-philo-gubb-correspondence-school-d:
Ellis Parker Butler's Philo Gubb, Correspondence-School Detective, printed in 1918 by Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York, follows a paper-hanger who studies with the Rising Sun Detective Agency's correspondence school. Walking close along the wall to avoid creaking floor boards, Philo Gubb practices his trade with earnest, comic confidence. Its cases include the hard-boiled egg, the pet, the eagle's claws, and the oubliette.

Later cases bring the un-burglars, the two-cent stamp, the chicken, the dragon's eye, and the progressive murder. A picture declares that in the deteckative line nothing sounds foolish. Readers of comic mystery will find a delightful, bumbling detective whose schooling never quite matches his cases.
29970-twenty-four-little-french-dinners-:
Cora Moore wrote Twenty-Four Little French Dinners and How to Cook and Serve Them, printed in New York in 1919 by E. P. Dutton and Company. Moore opens with the bugbear of American cookery: monotony. Supplies enough to feed a world are at hand, she says. Yet the American cook still serves the same flavors on the same days each week. Her sauces harden into lumps of grease when they cool.

Flavor, the handmaid of variety, true trails toward economy, and the appeal to the eye follow. Sauces, simple and otherwise, lead to the twenty-four little French dinners themselves, each with directions for preparing. Let Us Eat Fish closes the book. Moore writes for home cooks who want French variety without French fuss, in a clear, practical style.
30023-the-daughter-of-the-storage-and-ot:
William Dean Howells published The Daughter of the Storage and Other Things in Prose and Verse with Harper and Brothers, under copyrights of 1915 and 1916, and published in April 1916. Nineteen pieces make up the book, from the title story and A Presentiment to Captain Dunlevy's Last Trip, The Return to Favor, and Somebody's Mother. The Face at the Window, The Boarders, and Breakfast Is My Best Meal follow, with The Mother-Bird and The Amigo.

Black Cross Farm, The Critical Bookstore, and A Feast of Reason lead to City and Country in the Fall, Table Talk, and The Escapade of a Grandfather. Self-Sacrifice, a farce-tragedy, and The Night Before Christmas close the set. The title story opens with Forsyth helping his wife sort stored trunks, tables, and Colonial bureaus for a furnished country house.
30137-daisy-brooks-or-a-perilous-love:
Laura Jean Libbey opens a melodramatic romance on a warm, sultry evening in the southern part of West Virginia, as heat fades and fireflies wink in long grass. On a prosperous plantation, excitement stirs over the expected return of master Basil Hurlhurst with his bride. Workers in best attire watch the white pebbled road, while curtains at Whitestone Hall stand looped back for the homecoming.

George Munro held the 1883 copyright, and Ogilvie reissued the New York volume in 1911, with dramatic rights reserved by Libbey-Stillwell. Libbey, author of Parted on Her Bridal Tour and When His Love Grew Cold, writes in the popular sensation mode of her day. Daisy Brooks, the title heroine, enters a story promised by its subtitle to be a perilous love, full of feeling and sharp turns.
30474-they-also-serve:
Donald E. Westlake sets a Moon-base story from Analog, September 1961, around Captain Ebor, who guides a mail and supply launch toward a rocky base on the far side of the Moon. Keeping the bulk of the Moon between ship and Earth, he lands with practiced ease, stretches his walking tentacles, and suits up to meet base commander Darquelnoy.

An open ground car waits beside the ship, and its driver, also in a spacesuit, trades a sloppy salute with Ebor, since formal manners have faded on the periphery. Westlake opens with a wry note on vultures, which never kill anyone, hinting at service roles that look grim yet harm no one. The tale turns on duty far from home.
30825-the-camp-fire-girls-on-ellen-s-isl:
Hildegard G. Frey wrote this 1917 Camp Fire Girls tale, subtitled The Trail of the Seven Cedars, for the A. L. Burt Company in New York. Frey had already sent the same girls to the Maine woods, Onoway House, and school, and here the Winnebagos, including Hinpoha, gather at the Bradford home. The book opens on the hottest day of the hottest summer week of the hottest June on record, with cracked earth and panting dogs.

From that city heat the girls head for Ellen's Isle, where a launch scene on page eighty shows their arrival in lively style. Camp life, trails, and the seven cedars give the story its shape, with friendship and outdoor skill at its heart. Young readers get a wholesome summer adventure, full of heat, water, and the fun of a camp that feels like a second home.
3094-red-eve:
Haggard sets this romance in Suffolk in February 1346, under a hard frost. A young man and a maiden meet by the Blythburgh marshes near Dunwich. The reeds stand stark, the birds huddle swollen on the willows, and tide-broken ice marks the stream. Murgh the Messenger sails for the uttermost sea as their meeting takes place. First published in 1911, the novel is one of Haggard's late historical romances.

Love and peril drive the tale, played out on a coast shaped by sea and storm. The medieval world here comes through weather, work, and hard travel. Court pageantry takes second place to the facts of life in a cold border country.
30950-the-go-ahead-boys-and-the-treasure:
Ross Kay wrote this boys' adventure book for the Goldsmith Publishing Company in New York, with a 1916 copyright held by Barse and Hopkins. Kay had already written Dodging the North Sea Mines, With Joffre on the Battle Line, and The Go Ahead Boys on Smugglers' Island. Here the Go Ahead Boys sail for a treasure cave, in twenty-seven chapters from voyage begun to conclusion.

Chapter one opens aboard the brig Josephine, with all hands up anchor, sails loosed, and yards braced, as a boy and his companions watch the bustle. Later chapters bring a plucky feat, a superstitious cook, a code, a tropical storm, being adrift, an iron chest, an odd discovery, and a riddle worked out underground. It is a fast, wholesome sea and treasure tale for young readers who love codes, caves, and a crew that keeps going.
31036-the-lovers-assistant-or-new-art-of:
Henry Fielding wrote The Lovers Assistant, or, New Art of Love, first published in 1760. It is held here in an Augustan Reprint Society edition, publication number 89, from the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library at the University of California, Los Angeles, in 1961. It was edited, with an introduction, by Claude E. Jones, under general editors from Michigan, California, and other universities.

The reprint presents Fielding's eighteenth-century work in a scholarly modern edition, with notes and an introduction for students of the period. A note in the edition records what one of the most learned men of the age said on perusing the paraphrase. He thought it would serve better to a purpose the note leaves open. It is a slim, useful reprint for readers of Fielding and of Augustan literature.
31293-systematic-status-of-a-south-ameri:
John D. Lynch and Howard L. Freeman's 1966 paper, volume 17, number 10 of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series, settles the systematic status of the South American frog Allophryne ruthveni. Gaige described it in 1926 as a new genus and species of diminutive bufonid from British Guiana. Noble in 1931 placed it among toothless relatives of Centrolenella in the Hylidae, and Gallardo in 1965 suggested a leptodactylid of uncertain affinities.

Until now only the holotype and one paratype, both females, had been reported, leaving the family's position unsettled. A male collected in southern British Guiana by William A. Bentley in January 1962, with four more females in the American Museum, lets the authors re-examine the genus with skull and finger bones figured. The paper is a model of how one good specimen can steady a wandering name.
31406-cudjo-s-cave:
J. T. Trowbridge's novel Cudjo's Cave, published in Boston in 1864, is a Civil War-era tale built around a Quaker schoolmaster, Penn, and the people who cross his path. Its chapter titles trace the shape of the plot: a schoolmaster in trouble, ruffians, a secret cellar, a search for the missing, and a strange coat for a Quaker. Cudjo, Pomp, Carl, and Toby appear among the figures caught up in these events.

The book mixes adventure with the moral questions of its time, including an anti-slavery document noted among its chapters and scenes of southern hospitality set against danger. Readers who like period adventure will find a fast-moving story of hiding places, pursuits, and loyalties tested under wartime strain, told in the plain, direct style of a nineteenth-century popular novel.
31489-a-mad-love:
Bertha M. Clay's novel A Mad Love, published in Chicago by Donohue, Henneberry and Company, opens with a discontented beauty. Farmer Noel, a tall, stout, good-tempered man, stands in his farmyard calling for his niece Leone, here, there, and everywhere except just where she should be. At last Leone answers, and her voice, musical, deep, and full of pathos, startles as much as her uncle's loudness. She wishes he would not shout so loudly, since the people at Rashleigh can surely hear him.

Clay, author of Sunshine and Roses, Beyond Pardon, and Dora Thomas, builds the novel from Leone's discontent and the love that follows. Her romances were bestsellers of their day, mixing sentiment with strong incident. Readers of Victorian popular fiction will find a characteristic Clay tale: a heroine, a farm, a neighborhood listening in, and a love that refuses to stay reasonable.
31496-ditte-girl-alive:
Martin Anderson Nexö's Ditte, Girl Alive, translated from the Danish and published by Henry Holt and Company with copyright in 1920, follows a girl from birth into life. Part one opens with Ditte's family tree. It moves through events before her birth and the birth itself, then to her first step, her grandfather striking out afresh, the death of Søren Man, and the widow and the fatherless. Wise Maren and a visit to fairyland complete the early chapters.

Nexö, a Danish writer of working-class life, tells Ditte's story with attention to family, poverty, and endurance. The novel's scale is that of a life: small incidents accumulate into character. Readers will find a humane, realistic portrait of a girl growing up among hard circumstances, told without sentimentality and with faith in ordinary resilience.
31689-membership-drive:
Murray F. Yaco's short story, printed in Amazing Science Fiction Stories in July 1960, opens thirty million miles out, where Keeter monitors a planet's radio and television networks for two sleepless days and nights. Convinced there will be no language difficulty, he studies notes on English idioms and irregular verbs before landing.

The joke of the title follows: Keeter must pass the tests of a secret organization before he can join it. His carefully chosen wardrobe, including a helmet much like those seen on television, is part of the act. Readers get a comic first-contact tale about learning a culture from its broadcasts.
31796-logic-inductive-and-deductive:
William Minto's Logic, Inductive and Deductive, published by John Murray in London in 1915 after earlier printings from 1893, is a university manual for students of logic. Minto, late professor of logic at Aberdeen, sets out two aims that might seem at odds. They are putting logical forms on a historical basis and making logic a practical discipline.

The book's main purpose, as its preface states, is the organization of reason against error, with error in its various kinds as the basis of division. Readers get a compact, practical textbook that treats logic as a working art for clear thinking rather than a mere set of formulas.
32067-atom-drive:
Charles Fontenay's story, printed in If in April 1956, stages a space race between the tortoise and the hare. Its tagline warns that this hare uses dirty tricks to make sure the ending comes out different. The two spaceship crews are friendly enemies, sitting across a table for a final meal before launch. Outside the ports, Space Station 2 whirls on its axis, its sky a light-streaked blackness broken by Earth glare, creating artificial gravity.

At the table, Russo Baat, captain of the Mars Corporation freighter Marsward XVIII, teases Jonner Jons for deserting rockets for a hot-rod tow-job. Baat is a stout, red-faced man, and among the shrewdest captains in the business. Jons, grizzled and quiet, answers that times change, and even the Mars Corporation cannot stop that. Readers get a contest story, where an old hand's tow-job takes on a corporate freighter.
32083-st-patrick-s-eve:
Charles James Lever's short moral tale, published in London by Chapman and Hall in 1845, is addressed to his own children. In a dedication written at Templeogue on March 1, 1845, Lever says he wants the story to teach one truth: prosperity carries as many duties as adversity carries sorrows. Those blessed with much, he argues, are stewards of that bounty for the poor. Neglect of that duty is a grievous wrong.

The tale opens in its first era on March 16, the eve of St. Patrick, in a small village on the bank of Lough Corrib. The villagers are keeping their annual fair, giving a day to every kind of enjoyment. From that festive opening, Lever builds a story about landed responsibility, charity, and the harm that follows when those with power forget the people who depend on them. Drawings by Phiz accompany the text.
32125-rulers-of-india-lord-clive:
Colonel G. B. Malleson's Lord Clive, in the Rulers of India series edited by Sir William Wilson Hunter, was printed at the Clarendon Press, Oxford, in 1893. London and New York publishers issued it as well. The volume traces Robert Clive from his early years through his rise in India, in the series' compact biographical manner. An illustration of the Indian Empire fronts the book.

Its contents run from early years and southern India in 1744 to the war in the Karnatik. That war affected French and English settlements, and then the narrative turns to the fortunes of Robert Clive himself. Later chapters follow his campaigns and administration in the manner of a Victorian imperial life. Readers get a short, authoritative life of the man who founded British power in India, written by a soldier-historian for a general audience.
32216-the-adventures-of-the-u-202-an-act:
Baron Spiegel von und zu Peckelsheim, captain-lieutenant and commander of the U-202, published this narrative in New York with the Century Company in February 1917. It appeared by arrangement with the New York World. Its nine chapters run from Our First Success and An Eventful Night through The Sinking of the Transport and Rich Spoils. They continue to The Witch-Kettle, A Day of Terror, A Lively Chase, The British Bull-Dog, and Homeward Bound.

The narrative opens at the hunting grounds in the North Sea on April 12, with course northwest, wind southwest at strength three to four, sea strength three, and view good. Both machines run at high speed. The crew are comfortable in the conning tower. Readers get a First World War U-boat commander's own account, told in logbook style with a sailor's eye for weather, sea, and prey.
32389-favorite-fairy-tales-the-childhood:
Favorite Fairy Tales, published in New York and London in 1907 with illustrations by Peter Newell, gathers tales chosen as childhood favourites by well-known men and women. Jack the Giant-Killer, by Charles Perrault, was chosen by Yale president Arthur Twining Hadley, Columbia president Nicholas Murray Butler, and Harper's editor Henry M. Alden, among others. Cinderella, or The Little Glass Slipper, was chosen by Yale's Thomas R. Lounsbury and Columbia librarian J. H. Canfield.

Jack and the Bean-Stalk and The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood, also by Perrault, follow the same pattern, each with its list of choosers. The book thus pairs classic tales with a record of who loved them as children, from university presidents to authors and librarians. Newell's pictures make it a charming keepsake for families and collectors of children's books.
32396-oogie-finds-love:
Berkeley Livingston's tale, printed in Amazing Stories in November 1948, follows Oogie the Caveman in a wild bid to win Sala. The story opens in a wrestling ring, where Oogie lies underneath the Russian Bear while the crowd cries for the Bear's defeat. The referee, kneeling with his head near Oogie's shoulder, whispers that the boss wants to see Oogie after the match, a message no spectator can hear.

Oogie's path to Sala, the tale's framing note explains, also required a fierce battle with prehistoric Cro-Magnons. Livingston mixes stone-age adventure with modern show business, as clubbed women, cave fights, and a wrestling bout collide. The result is a broad, comic pulp story about strength, rivalry, and a caveman's stubborn pursuit of love.
32757-tried-for-her-life-a-sequel-to-cru:
Mrs. Emma D. E. N. Southworth continues the story of Sybil in this sequel to Cruel as the Grave, published in Philadelphia by T. B. Peterson and Brothers, entered in 1875. The title names Sybil's trial, and the narrative moves between her prison cell and the past that put her there.

Sybil, a beautiful woman of twenty, once used the devotion of a boy worshipper of fourteen to escape from a band and deliver herself to the authorities. Now her husband Lyon Berners visits her in prison, sings her to sleep with a guitar, and hopes for a respite and a voyage to Europe. Prison doors close at six in the afternoon, and Sybil must wait, happily unconscious of how much her cause still risks.
33322-observations-on-the-present-state-:
Thomas Baines's Observations on the Present State of the Affairs of the River Plate, printed in Liverpool in 1845, weighs the fate of the peoples along the River Plate. That river runs through South America. Baines opens with a line from Chateaubriand on a passive age watching a heroic struggle. His pamphlet argues that a nation must not be left to be sacrificed without peril to onlookers. His tone is urgent and political.

The pamphlet suits readers of South American history, offering a contemporary British view of war, trade, and diplomacy on the Plate. Its value lies in its immediacy, written while events were still unfolding. For students of the 1840s, it is a sharp, short source on a distant crisis as London saw it.
33852-british-butterflies-figures-and-de:
W. S. Coleman, author of Our Woodlands, Heaths, and Hedges, figures and describes every native species of British butterflies in this Routledge volume, with illustrations printed in colours by Edmund Evans. Coleman seeks to extend knowledge of, and thereby love for, those sunny creatures called butterflies. His work makes no pretence to a technically scientific character yet aims to be complete and accurate.

Contents give an account of butterfly development, structure, habits, localities, mode of capture, and preservation, with a figure and description for each species. Companion volumes in the uniform series cover common objects of the seashore and country, British birds, eggs and nests, moths, and beetles. Naturalists and collectors will enjoy a charming Victorian field guide, still useful for identification and local history.
33903-into-the-primitive:
Robert Ames Bennet published this adventure novel in 1908, with a frontispiece by Allen T. True. A castaway tale at heart, it strips its hero of city comforts and sets him to learn fire, woodcraft, bow, and club. Chapters trace his rise from wreck and hunger toward skill, order, and a new sense of manhood.

Leopards, snakes, fever, storms, and rival men test him at every turn, and a woman's presence sharpens the choice between old society shams and raw life. Bennet wrote for readers who liked survival tales with action on each page. The book still appeals as a brisk story of a man remade by the wild.
34104-four-phases-of-love:
Paul Heyse wrote this set of four love stories, translated by E. H. Kingsley and published in London and New York in 1857. The stories are Eye-Blindness and Soul-Blindness, Marion, La Rabbiata, and By the Banks of the Tiber. The first opens at a window over a little flower garden, where the blind daughter of a village sacristan stands in cool breeze.

Within, a blind boy of about fifteen plays wild melodies at an old spinet, turning his large eyes toward her. Heyse writes of love seen and unseen, with tenderness and craft. The volume offers a compact sample of Heyse's early short fiction.
34343-the-betrothal-a-sequel-to-the-blue:
The Betrothal is a fairy play in five acts and eleven scenes by Maurice Maeterlinck, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. Dodd, Mead printed it at New York in 1918. It is a sequel to The Blue Bird. Tyltyl is now sixteen years of age, and his cottage holds but one bed, his own.

The characters list six girls from whom a bride may be chosen: the wood-cutter's daughter, the butcher's daughter, the inn-keeper's daughter, the miller's daughter, the beggar's daughter, and the mayor's daughter. Joy, the veiled girl or white phantom, stands among them. Destiny, the Miser, and Light also appear, with Granny Tyl and Gaffer Tyl and a crowd of ancestors. The scenes run from the wood-cutter's cottage to the miser's cave, the abode of the ancestors, and the abode of the children. The play ends with the awakening.
35416-the-romance-of-biography-vol-2-of-:
The Romance of Biography, in its second volume, gathers memoirs of women loved and celebrated by poets. Mrs Jameson wrote the work, also issued as The Loves of the Poets. The third edition came from Saunders and Otley of London in 1837, in two volumes.

The series runs from the days of the troubadours to the present age. Its anecdotes show the influence of female beauty and virtue on men of genius. Jameson traces that influence over both the characters and the writings of poets. The second volume opens with Carew's Celia. Jameson had already written the Diary of an Ennuyée and lives of celebrated female sovereigns. Her Shakespeare heroines and court beauties belong to the same project. She built a career recovering women's lives from the margins of men's fame.
35523-only-one-love:
Charles Garvice wrote a romance printed at Chicago. Garvice had written Claire, Elaine, Her Heart's Desire, and Leola Dale's Fortune, among a long shelf of love tales. One summer's evening a young man was tramping through the Forest of Warden, the tale opens. Forest of Warden sounds strange, old fashioned, almost improbable, Garvice owns.

But thank Heaven there yet remain in over crowded England some spots still untouched by the greedy fingers of the destroyers, whom men call progress and civilization. To this grand old forest, whose dim shades echo the soft steps of deer and the coo of the wood pigeon, comes no tourist with hideous knapsack. Along a footpath the young man tramps, watching the sky shine red through the trees. A hidden heir and one true love drive Garvice's tale.
3628-the-kingdom-of-love:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox gathers poems in this 1909 volume, published in London by Gay and Hancock. Contents include The Kingdom of Love, Meg's Curse, Solitude, The Gossips, Platonic, Grandpa's Christmas, After the Engagement, A Holiday, False, Two Sinners, The Phantom Ball, and Words and Thoughts. A Servian legend and lighter pieces such as Peek-A-Boo also appear.

Wilcox writes in her popular, sentimental style, favoring love, loss, and moral reflection in clear, rhymed verse. Her speakers move from a tropical valley more lovely than Cashmere to quiet rooms of memory. The book suits readers who enjoy late Victorian popular poetry, earnest and musical, meant to be read aloud and remembered.
36439-the-story-of-an-untold-love:
Paul Leicester Ford wrote a novel copyrighted in 1897, here in its sixty fifth thousand from Grosset and Dunlap. Twenty six numbered chapters carry no titles. The story opens as a diary dated February 20, 1890. There is not a moment of my life that you have shared with me, the writer tells the beloved, which I cannot recall with sunlit distinctness.

Joys and sorrows have faded into mere memories, he writes, while you alone set pulse and thought throbbing. Ford was a historian and novelist of New York society. His untold love is confessed only in the diary. The book's huge printing shows its hold on readers of the nineties.
3653-the-guns-of-bull-run-a-story-of-the:
Joseph Altsheler opens his Civil War series with this novel of the war's eve and its first great battle. The principal characters include Harry Kenton, a lad who fights for the South, and his cousin Dick Mason, who fights for the North. Other figures include a Southern messenger, a Pennsylvania colonel, and officers and merchants on both sides.

The story follows Harry from Kentucky and the border country to the armies gathering in Virginia, ending at Bull Run. Altsheler writes for young readers, mixing camp life, scouting, and battle with family loyalty divided by war. The novel suits readers who enjoy historical adventure and want the Civil War told as a boys' story first.
3771-cynthia-s-revels-or-the-fountain-of:
Ben Jonson wrote this satirical comedy for the court, where the goddess Cynthia, a figure for Queen Elizabeth herself, presides over a world drunk on self love. Gallants and ladies crowd her court, sipping from a fountain that makes each one adore his own wit, dress, and verse. A pair of would be wits trade play particles, pretty scraps of borrowed poetry, hoping to embroider their talk into fashion.

Jonson aims his sharpest darts at vanity, flattery, and the fashion for stolen phrases, while true poets watch from the edge. The play mixes verse, masque, and sharp dialogue, and its jokes bite the very courtiers who first applauded them. Readers who enjoy satire will find a lively, if demanding, comedy of a court admiring itself in a mirror.
40180-a-woman-s-love:
Woman Love is a tale in the third volume of the works of Amelia Opie, issued at Philadelphia in 1848. Crissy and Markley published the complete works in three volumes in that city. Contents of this volume open with Temper, a tale, at page five of the book. Woman Love follows at page 175 in the list of the volume.
