A Wife Duty, being a continuation of Woman Love, comes next at page 209 in the contents. The Two Sons, The Opposite Neighbour, and Love, Mystery, and Superstition follow in the list. The volume closes with Illustrations of Lying, in all its branches, a moral essay in chapters. Opie, a Norwich novelist of the age of Scott, wrote tales of feeling and conduct. Her American collected edition carried her name across the Atlantic for a new generation of readers.
40428-a-sermon-delivered-before-his-exce:
A Sermon is a state day speech by Mark Hopkins, head of Williams College. He spoke it ere Governor Edward Everett and the law house of Massachusetts. The day was the year start vote feast of January second, eighteen thirty nine. State press men at Boston printed the speech in that same year. The senate gave thanks and begged a copy for print the next day.

Its text is the Acts line that we ought to obey God rather than men. Man was made for more than to make or heed mere human laws, it opens. His cure and joy rest in heed of the laws of God alone. No power can bind a man to break those laws, the speech holds. State rule draws its claim from God set place, not from pact.
40443-the-spirit-of-god-as-fire-the-glob:
The Spirit of God as Fire puts forward a bold claim about heaven by D Mortimore, a physician, published in New York in 1870. The full title joins the claim: the globe within the sun is our heaven. Mortimore argues the case from scripture and from astronomy together.

Early chapters treat the soul's immortality and the office of the sun. The sun gives light and heat to the whole system. Fixed stars, he argues, are suns like ours. Scripture is then searched for proof of a globe inside the sun. Measurements follow: the city is large enough to hold all the saved. Angels, the resurrection, and the final judgment close the argument. Appeals to ministers and to the unconverted end the book. It is a curious survival of an age when laymen still built heavens out of telescopes and Bibles.
41137-dead-man-s-love:
Dead Man's Love is a novel by Tom Gallon, author of Tatterley, published by Brentano's in New York. The chapter titles tell its kind: the missing man, a little white ghost, an appointment with death, and William Capper comes to life. The narrator tells his own story from inside a prison cell's memory.

He came out of Penthouse Prison one May morning at four o'clock, by way of the roof. A fire in the night, a broken hose, and a line of buckets put the trusted prisoner at the least guarded end; he set down his bucket and ran. Raised by Uncle Zabdiel Blowfield, he is the convict with a buried past recounting his story.
41720-prisons-and-prayer-or-a-labor-of-l:
Prisons and Prayer, or A Labor of Love, is a prison evangelist memoir by Elizabeth Wheaton. A portrait of Mother Wheaton fronts the account of her gospel work. She tells of nearly twenty two years seeking the lost in prisons and reformatories. Stockades, rescue homes, saloons and dives, streets, and railway trains fill her field.

Verses from the Psalms and from Matthew head her title page as her warrant. In prison, and ye came unto me, is the text she lived by for decades. Converted prisoners and temperance rescues fill her record of the labour of love. American revival history keeps Mother Wheaton among its striking women workers.
42051-akra-the-slave:
A verse tale by Wilfrid Wilson Gibson, published at London in 1910. Elkin Mathews issued the slim volume. A preface in verse looks back six years. Gibson wrote the story, he says, with eastern light still in his eyes. A sea-girt town of minarets haunts the memory. Its dark alleys led to a great white dome.

Akra himself tells the tale in monologue. He stands captive before a king who holds death over him. He refuses to tremble or grovel. His memories run back to childhood at his mother's breast. Death stalked the cave mouth even then. Panthers, snakes, and jungle tracks shaped his courage. The poem turns his defiance into a meditation on fear. Love's story, the preface promises, never grows old.
42112-the-yellowstone-national-park-hist:
Hiram Martin Chittenden, a captain in the Army Corps of Engineers, writes the history and wonders of the first national park. The Robert Clarke Company issued his book at Cincinnati in 1895. Maps, views, and portraits fill it.

He dedicates the work to John Colter and James Bridger. Both men pioneered in the upper Yellowstone country. His preface recalls a camp at the Forks of the Madison. Twenty-five years back, a party there finished the first full tour of the region. They agreed that government protection alone could save it. Within eighteen months the Act of Dedication became law. Chittenden tells how local hostility yielded to a wiser patriotism. His book joined a soldier's record to a park guide.
42133-bobs-a-girl-detective:
Bobs, A Girl Detective is a girls' tale by Carol Norton from 1928. Four girls of a proud house face a crash in their luck. The house is the Vandergrift home on Long Island in New York. Gloria, the eldest, laughs in the face of the fall.

Gwen, her sister, taps her shoe and scowls at the jest. The girls must ask what the house will do next to live. One of them is Bobs, who turns her wits to the hunt for clues. The front plate shows her at work while a man is out. The tale mixes home strife with the thrill of the chase. It is a bright, fast book for the young of its day.
42822-semiramis-a-tale-of-battle-and-of-:
Edward Peple wrote a historical novel copyrighted in 1907, subtitled a tale of battle and of love, and dedicated to the Little Padre. His preface warns that the history of Semiramis is confounded with ancient religion and superstition. Little authentic fact, he says, can be gleaned from it. Legends passed from father to son among Syrians and Persians before Greeks recorded them.

Peple jokes that Greek writers seldom let mere truth block a good story. Contents move from the raising of a siege to the building of a city. The governor of Syria, a fish goddess, and a prayer to Dagon follow. Later chapters cover an army on the march and a war queen's prophecy.
42923-the-doctor-s-christmas-eve:
James Lane Allen, who wrote The Choir Invisible, stands behind this grave novel of a father's hidden life. Macmillan printed The Doctor's Christmas Eve at New York in November 1910. Its second title is Francis of Assisi, and a Latin tag says my secret is mine.

The Children of Desire open part one. When a Son Finds Out about His Father turns the plot. The Books of the Year and the Book of the Years weigh a life's reading. Evergreen and Thorn Tree close the part. Two winter snowbirds at a window open part two. Four in a Cage, the Realm of Midnight, and When a Father Finds Out about a Son end the dark design.
42970-the-gates-of-india-being-an-histor:
The Gates of India is a historical narrative by Colonel Sir Thomas Holdich, published by Macmillan in 1910 with maps. Holdich was a frontier surveyor who knew the ground at first hand. His gates are the passes and coasts by which the world has entered India through Afghanistan and Baluchistan across three thousand years.

The chapters march in chronological order. Greece and Persia open the story, then Alexander in the Kabul valley, Chinese pilgrims at the northern gates, medieval geographers in Seistan, and Arab traders at the gates of Makran. English, American and French explorers close the procession: Christie and Pottinger, Masson, Moorcroft, Burnes and Ferrier. Holdich writes imperial geography as a single long argument: whoever would understand India must first understand the doors by which everyone has come to it.
43071-the-alternative:
George Barr McCutcheon wrote The Alternative, a novel published in April nineteen hundred and nine with pictures by Harrison Fisher. McCutcheon had written The Husbands of Edith and The Purple Parasol. The tale opens in a storm at a smart New York club.

A shrieking wind and sleety snow beat at the windows of a club for college men. Its members, the narrator jokes, seem born to membership through grandfathers of old classes. Chapter heads promise the Van Pyckes, a young lady's entrance, and an amazing marriage. A secretary goes home, and a first holiday follows. Society manners and young love carry the short opening movement.
43298-the-riddle-and-the-ring-or-won-by-:
Gordon MacLaren wrote a mystery from Top Notch Magazine, printed at New York in 1911 by Street and Smith. The little man in black opens the tale, then an amazing offer and panic. The emerald ring and the power of avarice drive the plot. As in a dream, new grace and dignity, and the gates of chance follow.

A woman in distress, Shirley Rives, hide and seek, and puzzled heads fill the middle. The wheel of fortune, followed, and the girl who vanished raise the stakes. The touch of cold steel, by force of arms, the empty house, and the face in the candlelight crowd the close. Was it possible the persecution had begun again, the hero asks, after three weeks of peace. A ring and a riddle keep the pages turning.
4344-marie-a-story-of-russian-love:
Alexander Pushkin wrote this short novel of Russian love, here translated by Marie H. de Zielinska as Marie. Its contents run from the sergeant of the guards and the guide to the fortress, the duel, love, and the rebel Pugachev. Later chapters bring an assault, a separation, a siege, the rebel camp, and a sentence.

The translator's note recalls Pushkin's life: born at Saint Petersburg in 1799, entering the foreign affairs service at twenty-one, and exiled after his Ode to Liberty. The novel itself, known in English as The Captain's Daughter, sets a young officer's love against Pugachev's revolt. It is Pushkin's prose at its clearest and most humane.
44208-the-hive:
The Hive is a book of essays and meditations by Will Levington Comfort, published by the Doran Company of New York in 1918. Comfort, the author of Midstream and Child and Country, dedicated the volume to Mary with a fragment of verse about soft gold and pomegranate red.

The contents mix the personal and the cosmic. Essays treat North Americans, the conquest of fears, the stuff of comrades, and the values of letter writing. Others take up the new dancing, old pictures in red, the abbot, the artist unleashed, and work in short stories. A late sequence runs through imagination, boys and dogs, the man who found peace, and the mating mystery. A chapter of letters and a résumé close the book. Comfort writes as a spiritual essayist, insisting that a spiritual thing can only be pictured where it has broken through into the world of matter.
44395-at-the-court-of-the-ami-r-a-narrat:
At the Court of the Amir is a tale of life in a shut land. John Gray, a healer, was the chief's own surgeon in that land. The chief was the strong man who ruled the Afghans at that time. The book came out in London in the year 1895.

Gray owns he took up the pen at his house's wish, not his own. The land was hard to reach and but dimly known to his kin. Great shifts in its rule had come with the new chief's reign. Those shifts made a tale of its life worth the trade's while, he holds. His book was built from notes he sent home to his bride to be. The road in, the forts, and the tribes on the way fill the first part. Coins struck by hand and the chief's own face dress the book.
44829-rada-a-belgian-christmas-eve:
Rada, a Belgian Christmas Eve, is a war poem by Noyes, the famed bard of sea songs and old inns. It came out at London in the mid war years, with four prints from the war pains of a great Spanish hand. A list at its front names his past books of verse and tale.

Its gift word is a prayer for a world at war. Thou whose deep ways are in the sea, it runs, whose foot steps are not known. To night a world that turned from thee waits at thy throne. The towers of pride we raised, where scoff fops brawl, and the wee false gods we praised, the night is on them all. The fool has said, it tolls twice, and we who deemed him wise believed the claim.
45080-the-pan-angles-a-consideration-of-:
The Pan-Angles is a political book by Sinclair Kennedy, printed by Longmans, Green and Company in 1915. Its subtitle calls it a consideration of the federation of the seven English-speaking nations. The hosted copy is the second impression. The book carries a map. Its prefatory note thanks publishers and authors for leave to quote from works on kindred themes.

Among the books Kennedy quotes are Colonial Nationalism by Richard Jebb, Imperial Architects, and Federations and Unions. His own argument, as the title states it, is for drawing the English-speaking peoples into one federation. Kennedy writes as an advocate: the prefatory thanks show the shelf of federation literature he builds on. The volume is a document of the movement for an English-speaking union, made while the war was testing every bond it praised.
46402-harry-blount-the-detective:
Flanagan's Harry Blount, the Detective, or The Martin Mystery Solved, appeared as number 61 of the Sunset Series. Ogilvie of New York sold it for twenty-five cents; the issue is dated August 16, 1893, and the story was copyrighted in 1891. Twenty-seven chapters make the tale. It opens on a May morning at Hanley Hall in Lancashire, the seat of Stafford. Stafford, an ardent lover of nature, frowns over breakfast because the mail is late.

The delayed mail brings an American letter, and the frown turns to teasing. Stafford tells his daughter Kate, a dark-eyed girl of nineteen, to prepare to receive her husband-to-be at almost any minute. The letter, mailed two days before sailing from New York, says the man is coming to claim her. Wife and daughter demand the meaning while Stafford laughs at their suspense.
46428-the-natural-philosophy-of-love:
The Natural Philosophy of Love is a study of sex by Remy de Gourmont. Ezra Pound translated it, adding a postscript. Boni and Liveright issued it in New York in 1922. The contents open with love's general psychology. Love is treated as a law of nature throughout. Man's place in nature is set beside the beasts. Human and animal minds are held to be one.

Later chapters trace the scale of the sexes. Asexual increase and the birth of two sexes follow. Hermaphrodite and self-born forms are surveyed. Sexual difference in insects gets long treatment. Tiny males and ruling females crowd those pages. Birds and beasts are then compared. The pair and its bond close the argument. Gourmont writes as a cool man of science.
46520-secret-service-or-recollections-of:
Secret Service, or Recollections of a City Detective is a book of case tales by Andrew Forrester, published in London by Ward and Lock in 1864. The title page calls it never before published. The contents list a detective's working life. My Great Electioneering Trick opens the set. Mistaken Identity and An Unscrupulous Woman follow. An incendiary gang takes a long tale of its own. A railway accident, queried in its title, stands in the mid run.

The virtue of an American passport and a grand railway plant come later. Who was the greatest criminal is posed as a chapter of its own. The missing will and the workhouse doctor close the list. Forrester writes as a man of the force, with the city as his beat. The tales are among the first English detective case books in print.
46521-forty-years-among-the-indians-a-tr:
Daniel W Jones wrote Forty Years Among the Indians. The Juvenile Instructor Office issued it at Salt Lake City in 1890. Jones calls it a true yet thrilling tale. His years among Native peoples and Mexicans fill it. Friends urged him to write, his preface says. He kept no journal through those years.

A few saved letters aid his memory here. The plain, simple truth is his aim, he states. Truth without malice toward anyone is his rule. That rule will prove hard to keep, he admits. Unlearned readers will grasp his plain words, he hopes. No paid hand smoothed his style for print. Crossing the plains opens the story proper. A Mormon frontiersman's own record, the book tells of scouts, missions, and wars as one plain man recalled them late in life.
4659-lady-hester-or-ursula-s-narrative:
Charlotte M. Yonge tells Lady Hester, or Ursula's Narrative, through Ursula herself, writing by desire of her brothers and sisters. If reports of their strange family history come down to later generations, she says, the thing should be properly understood. Old times at Trevorsham seem remote, and Jaquetta laughs that they could not be happier than since, while Fulk reminds Ursula that all was not always smooth, even then.

Chapters run from Sault St. Pierre and Trevorsham, through a peerage case and Skimping's farm, to Spinney Lawn, the white doe's warning, hunting, and duck shooting. Trevor's legacy closes the set. Ursula recalls back-boards and stocks, French in the schoolroom, and other childhood troubles. Readers get a gentle Victorian family story, told as a sister's record, about home, kinship, and a past that still shapes the present.
47056-cyprus-historical-and-descriptive:
Cyprus, Historical and Descriptive, adapts a German travel book by Franz von Loher for English readers. Joyner added much fresh matter and two maps to the English version. Allen published it in London in eighteen seventy eight, the year Britain took the island. Its opening explains why Cyprus had suddenly become news in England.

Von Loher journeyed the length and breadth of the island just before the change. He writes of its soil, its crops, its scenery, and its people's daily work. The aim is plain facts over the old tales of chivalry and romance. An appendix adds history and figures on the island from other sources. Climate, fertile soil, and fine landscape are praised by the classic writers quoted. The book meant to correct false notions of the Cypriotes then current.
48194-ryerson-memorial-volume-prepared-o:
J George Hodgins prepared the Ryerson Memorial Volume for the unveiling of the Ryerson statue on the Queen's Birthday in 1889 at Toronto. Hodgins was deputy minister of education for Ontario. The statue stands in the grounds of the Education Department. Warwick and Sons printed the book. A print of the statue heads the volume.

Hodgins chaired the statue committee and spoke on the day. He calls himself a lifelong friend and fellow worker of Ryerson. His task was to trace the roots of the school system of Ontario. He holds that Ryerson's hand joined its base rules and forces into one charter. That charter still rules the schools of the day, he says. Reports and past facts fill the latter part of the book.
48263-life-of-isaac-mason-as-a-slave:
Life of Isaac Mason as a Slave is the memoir of a man who escaped bondage in Maryland. Mason printed the book at Worcester, Massachusetts, in 1893. Senator George Hoar supplies a letter praising Mason's honesty. The contents run from first memories to a visit to Haiti.

Mason opens in a small town in Kent County, Maryland, where he was born in 1822. Friends who heard him lecture pressed him to write his story, he says. He tells it in a plain, matter of fact way, asking pardon for his lack of schooling. Chapters cover a new home, the escape itself, and life in the land of freedom. A flying visit to Haiti closes the tale. The book is one of the later slave narratives, printed for northern readers.
48580-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-30:
Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, number 305 of the new series, is the weekly issue for Saturday, the third of November 1849. William and Robert Chambers conducted the journal in Edinburgh, and the price was three halfpence. The Chambers brothers also edited Information for the People and an educational course.

The leading article, Tracings of the North of Europe, begins a voyage to Copenhagen. The traveller had set apart the summer for a tour of German cities and Italy, after a pleasant excursion in Rhineland and Switzerland the year before. But the continent, in the year of revolutions, was in such a volcanic state that no comfort could be had walking over hot cinders. So he turned his thoughts to Scandinavia, a group of countries little visited by the English. Their coolness, usually counted against them, here became their merit. The journal mixed such travel with instruction for working readers.
48583-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-30:
Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, number 306 of the new series, dated Saturday, November 10, 1849, was the famous cheap weekly run by William and Robert Chambers, priced at three halfpence. The number opens with an essay called Appearances. It asks whether seeming good matters when being good is the rule.

The essay argues that the pure must also look pure, or vice gains a hiding place and hypocrisy loses its sting. Around such improving essays the journal packed tales, facts, and verse for working readers. Chambers built an empire on the idea that plain people wanted real reading at a penny price.
48864-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-30:
Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, number 307 of its new series, is a weekly magazine issue dated Saturday, November 17, 1849. It was conducted by William and Robert Chambers and sold for three halfpence. The brothers also edited works of popular information and education, as the masthead notes.

The issue opens with a travel piece, Tracings of the North of Europe, covering Elsinore and Gothenburg. The writer leaves Copenhagen for Elsinore on the last day of June, with two companions, in a horse-drawn carriage. Their route passes a famed Danish palace where the king was then living. The piece remarks on the modest, private style of King Frederick the Seventh. Half the rulers of Europe, it notes, were then in the grip of revolution, while the Danish king gave his mind to ancient burial mounds found near his home.
49150-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-30:
Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, number 308 of the new series, was dated Saturday, November 24, 1849, and sold for a penny and a half. William and Robert Chambers ran the weekly for a broad reading public. The lead piece, The Half-Boarder, is by the wife of Alaric Watts, whose name appears with the tale.

The sketch follows a girl who is often the eldest child in a poor but genteel home. The girl does house work, nurses a sick mother, cheers a worn father, and teaches her younger brothers and sisters. The story follows her path until a family crisis forces a plea for help from rich kin. The issue shows how cheap weeklies mixed social comment with fiction.
50034-tragedies-of-the-white-slave:
Tragedies of the White Slaves is an exposé by Lytle, issued at Chicago in 1909. Lytle was a special investigator for the press. Ten true stories make up the book. Each shows a different trap for girls. The want ad and the stage agency are two. A maternity house and a little immigrant figure too. The tale of Ella Gingles is told in her own words. Her trial is reported by the author's son.

The foreword cites five thousand girls lost each year in Chicago. Police and vigilance leagues stand behind the figure. Such books fed the white slavery panic of the age. Reformers used them to push new laws. The Mann Act followed within a year. Its tales are grim, lurid, and earnest at once.
50138-doomsday-eve:
A science fiction novel by Robert Moore Williams. Ace Books published it at New York with a 1957 copyright. The cover copy promises a split-second race with world's end. War threatens humanity's total destruction in the story. Midst of it, mysterious new people suddenly appear. They perform incredible deeds and vanish at will.

Kurt Zen, an American intelligence officer, hunts them. The cast list pairs him against Nedra, a new person with old emotions. Cuso pits Oriental cunning against Western ingenuity. Zen finds the hidden lair and waits there captive. The enemy readies a super missile to end all life. Only the source of the new people's power can stop it. Ace sold such tales in cheap paperback racks.
50176-the-pride-of-eve:
Warwick Deeping sets a tale of women and pride at a country house called Fernhill. Cassell and Company issued the novel in September 1914. A popular edition followed in 1926.

The contents open with the coming of Guinevere. Lynette feeds the fairies, and Guinevere has her portrait painted. An importunate beggar calls. Eve enters the wilderness in chapter five. Life at Fernhill and tea in the wilderness fill the middle of part one. Eve speaks out, and a man stands in the moonlight. Part two moves to Bosnia Road and earning a living. The suffragette gets a chapter. Eve determines to leave Bosnia Road and pursues experience. The rosery at Fernhill, the text says, would please a Persian poet on a scented June day.
50902-how-to-be-a-detective:
Old King Brady, the famed detective of story papers, set down his trade rules in a small book for boys. Frank Tousey of New York entered it in 1902. Brady says at the start that no wand can turn a school boy into a detective. The work must be learned, like any other work, and each case is new.

He first lists what a good detective needs. The list calls for pluck and good health, strict honesty, a fair schooling, and skill with tongues. It adds the art of reading men and the hard art of disguise. Brady then tells how he made two boys into detectives, and he adds tales of well known men of the trade. The tone is bluff and kind, aimed at the vast crowd of boys who read his tales.
5103-a-zola-dictionary-the-characters-of:
J. G. Patterson's reference book unlocks Emile Zola's great cycle of twenty novels about the Rougon-Macquart family under the Second Empire. It opens with a biographical and critical introduction and synopses of each novel's plot, then gives an alphabetical dictionary of the cycle's characters, with a map and a family genealogy.

Anyone reading Zola will use it to keep track of a huge cast across many volumes, from shopkeepers and miners to financiers and politicians. The book works as a companion for a first read and as a finding aid for later study, making one of the largest achievements of nineteenth-century fiction easier to follow.
5125-last-poems-translations-from-the-bo:
Laurence Hope, the pen name of Adela Florence Cory Nicolson, translated these poems from Indian love poetry, presenting them as her last collection. Dedicated to her husband Malcolm Nicolson, the verses speak of longing, separation. Devotion fills the verses, in the voice of Indian lovers, rendered in English lyric forms.

Hope lived in India and drew on its poetry and imagery throughout her work. These short, passionate poems show her at her most direct. They offer readers a window into how a British writer of the period imagined and honoured Indian feeling, in verses meant to be read aloud and felt rather than studied.
51780-the-olive:
The Olive is a monograph by Bitting, printed at Chicago with copyright in 1920. Bitting worked as bacteriologist for the Glass Container Association of America, at its research laboratory on Michigan Avenue. The association issued the book. Its opening claim is large: no tree or fruit offers more interest than the olive.

To grasp the olive's many sides, Bitting says, one must know ancient legends, art, botany, chemistry, cooking, medicine, and cosmetics. The fruit served peoples as food and symbol alike. Its origin, following De Candolle, lies in Asia Minor, from Syria to Greece. It has been cultivated for more than 4,000 years, the longest span for any tree. Genesis tells how the dove brought Noah an olive leaf.
52365-the-sayings-of-mrs-solomon-being-t:
Helen Rowland wrote The Sayings of Mrs Solomon, being the confessions of the seven hundredth wife, issued in New York by Dodge Publishing Company with copyright in nineteen thirteen. Rowland had earlier written The Widow and Reflections of a Bachelor Girl. Eight books fill the volume, from Greeting to Book of Songs. A front line holds that a woman need know but one man well to understand all men.

Hearken, my daughter, and give ear unto my wisdom, the greeting opens in mock Bible style. Question me not whence I have learned of man, his secrets, it says. Men are of but one pattern, but women are as the Yale lock, no two alike, it holds. Book of Husbands, Book of Flirts, and Book of Damsels follow. Book of Bachelors, Book of Sirens, and Book of Admonitions fill the middle. Humour readers get sharp wedlock wit in proverb form.
525-youth-a-narrative:
Joseph Conrad lets Marlow recall his first voyage east in this short tale, told round a mahogany table in England. Young Marlow, second mate of a barque bound for Bangkok, faces fire, wreck, and a long boat passage, yet remembers the voyage as pure youth. Directors, lawyers, and old seamen listen as he tells it.

Conrad writes with lyric warmth, catching how hardship feels like glory at twenty. The sea, the ship, and the Eastern ports glow in Marlow's memory. The tale endures as a celebration of young daring, and as the first full portrait of Conrad's great narrator.
5320-taken-alive:
E. P. Roe's Taken Alive, volume eleven of his works, gathers stories with an autobiography, under the heading A Native Author Called Roe. Its contents include Taken Alive itself, in chapters on something before unknown. A visitor at the mine, thwarted hopes, and what Brandt saw follow. Christmas Eve follows, with Found Yet Lost, Love in the Wilderness, and Love at Home after it.

Roe writes moral, domestic stories of American life, with illustrations in the original. The volume offers readers both fiction and the author's own account of his career. It shows why Roe was one of the most popular American novelists of his day.
53416-only-a-girl-s-love: Only a Girl's Love is a romance novel by Charles Garvice, issued by Street and Smith of New York as number 215 of the Eagle Series. The copy shown here opens with the series' own pages rather than the tale: a weekly line of copyright fiction for news dealers. Its long list of titles is ruled by Mrs Georgie Sheldon, from Queen Bess to The Masked Bridal. Of the story itself, the front matter tells nothing beyond the title.
53852-letters-to-catherine-e-beecher-in-:
Letters to Catherine Beecher, in Reply to an Essay on Slavery and Abolitionism, is a set of public letters by the abolitionist Angelina Grimké. Isaac Knapp printed them in Boston in 1838, revised by the author. Beecher's essay had been addressed to Grimké herself. The first letter, dated from Brookline in June 1837, states the fundamental principle of abolitionists, and Grimké writes as she travels.

Incessantly occupied in prosecuting a mission, she says, she can reply only by letters thrown from her pen on the road. Beecher thought her ill-informed about the feelings of Christian women at the North. Grimké answers that northern women hold abolitionist principles, though they condemn abolitionist measures. A passage preserved in the copy states the core argument. To steal a man is to rob him of himself. It matters not whether it be done in Guinea or Carolina.
54946-cottage-on-the-curve:
Mary Lamers wrote Cottage on the Curve, published by the Bruce Publishing Company of Milwaukee in 1945. Lamers drew the sketches herself and dedicated the book to her mother. Its foreword, written in the summer of 1945, sets the tone. The story was written in time of war, in the memory of peace, when children played on the shores of Oak Lake and have since sailed away to battle.

The chapters follow one summer at the lake. Jane Murray empties her desk on the last day of school. Family puzzles follow: who peppered the cake, a purse in the trash pile, and a turtle who towed the boat. Grandma brings presents, a dog named Buick plays detective, and Billy battles a storm. The book closes with good-by summer. Lamers wrote a gentle children's story of a lakeside household, offered to wartime readers as a picture of the peace they remembered.
55663-the-sauciest-boy-in-the-service-a-:
The Sauciest Boy in the Service is a boys' sea story by Gordon-Stables, a Royal Navy surgeon. Ward, Lock published it in London in 1911. Its subtitle calls it a story of pluck and perseverance. Henry Austin drew coloured illustrations for the volume. A preface says the hero is drawn from real life. Most of the adventures come from the author's own experience. The scenery is painted from nature, the preface adds. The contents open with The Glamour of the Ocean.

Later chapters bring a mutiny aboard the ship Macbeth. A hurricane leaves the crew as castaways on Great Snake Island. Sunken gold and a career at Sydney follow the wreck. Kep, a dog, cuts off a leg in one chapter title. A frontispiece shows two men in a deadly knife embrace. The tale is a sailor's yarn of service, storm, and rescue.
55734-miss-beecher-s-housekeeper-and-hea:
Miss Beecher's Housekeeper and Healthkeeper, issued at New York in 1873 by Harper and Brothers, holds five hundred recipes for cheap and healthful cooking. The full title adds many rules for health and happiness. Doctors of all classes passed the book, the title claims. Parts treat food, markets, and care of meats in turn.

Chapter One gives health rules for food and drink and the measures used. Chapter Two treats beef, veal, mutton, pork, fowl, and fish cuts. Salt beef, hams, lard, and sausage meat get plain steps. Chapter Three treats stews of beef, mutton, fowl, and more. Irish stew, French pot au feu, and Spanish olla podrida sit side by side. Soups fill the next chapter. The book joins kitchen work to health in one home guide.
55876-in-the-prison-city-brussels-1914-1:
Twells wrote In the Prison City, Brussels, 1914 to 1918, a personal narrative, in 1919. Andrew Melrose of London put out the book. Twells gives it to the companion whose care and sympathy lightened the dark years. That care, he says, comforted the lives of many sufferers in the city. Chapter one opens with thanks to heaven for a sane country at last. Twells and his companion crossed into Belgium early in August 1914.

They came from terror-stricken France, where Paris had shown panic like revolution days. Letters of credit were worthless, and stranded travelers lived on a hotel keeper's faith. Belgium, by contrast, met the German attack with calm confidence at the frontier. Its forts were weak and its border had been treacherously crossed, Twells says.
56175-the-gray-scalp-or-the-blackfoot-br:
The Gray Scalp, or The Blackfoot Brave is Number Two Hundred and Five in Beadle's Dime Novels, issued at New York by Beadle and Company. Front pages advertise Number Two Hundred and Six, Buckskin Bill, or The White Demon of the Woods, by Guy Greenwood. That tale is called a richly racy romance of the woods. A forest heroine is its boast.

Buckskin Bill is rough as a bear and gentle as a fawn, the ad says. He is brave as a lion yet afraid of a young girl's frown. His daughter is his perfect contrast, grace and bravery in one. A captain, the dreaded Demon Slayer, and an Indian chief fill that tale's cast, in the terms of the day. The Gray Scalp itself belongs to the same line of Blackfoot country romances. Fast action and strange incident are the stock of the series.
56306-living-the-radiant-life-a-personal:
George Wharton James wrote Living the Radiant Life, a personal story, with the book listed among his works for nineteen sixteen. James had written Quit Your Worrying and books on California and the Southwest. The front pages list his works, with prices and praise.

James gives thanks for a friend who, in all the years he had known her, never failed to shine. She sent out what was sweet, pure, helpful, and kind. The book tells how James learned to live in that same bright way. It mixes life story with counsel, in the warm tone of his talks.
56720-lanagan-amateur-detective:
Edward H Hurlbut wrote Lanagan, Amateur Detective, with illustrations by Frederic Dorr Steele, issued in New York by Sturgis and Walton Company in nineteen thirteen. Ten chapters fill the book. A front plate shows two more shots tearing through and spraying the men with splinters. Jack Lanagan of the San Francisco Enquirer is the hero. Chapter one is Whither Thou Goest.

Lanagan was conceded to have arrived as the premier police reporter of San Francisco, the tale opens. The honour came not solely from brilliant newspaper feats in his field, it adds. An entente let him call half the patrolmen on the force by name, it notes. Chapters treat The Paths of Judgment, The Conspiracy of One, and Whom the Gods Destroy. The Ambassador Stick Pin, The Pendelton Legacy, and At the End of the Long Night follow. Mystery fans get a reporter sleuth in ten linked cases.
5734-life-in-the-grey-nunnery-at-montrea:
Sarah Richardson presents Life in the Grey Nunnery at Montreal as an authentic narrative of convent life. Chapters move from parentage and a father's marriage through the white nunnery, the nursery, a slave for life, confirmation, the grey nunnery, an orphan's home, and confession and sorrow of no avail. Later chapters promise alone with the dead, the sick nun, and at last the joy of freedom.

Readers should treat the book as a period exposé narrative, a popular genre that claimed inside knowledge of closed institutions. Its power comes from personal testimony, whether readers accept its claims or read it as polemic. Historians of religion, gender, and anti-Catholic literature will find it a vivid example of nineteenth-century convent tales and the fears they fed.
57527-the-great-white-way-a-record-of-an:
Albert Paine shaped the notes of Nicholas Chase into a tale of a sea trip south. The book came out in New York in 1901. Chase led the trip and told of love as well as finds. Drawings and maps from his note book fill the pages.

The yacht Billowcrest sails through calm seas and gloom toward the far south. The crew face storms, ice, and long dark nights on the way. Chase mixes facts of the trip with bold claims of finds. The book reads as a brisk tale of quest and risk at sea.
57876-harrington-a-story-of-true-love:
Harrington, A Story of True Love, was issued at Boston by Thayer and Eldridge in 1860. Its author is named only as the writer of What Cheer and A Tale of Lynn. A long motto from Malory heads the title page. That motto lists chivalry, courtesy, love, murder, hate, virtue, and sin.

Do after the good and leave the evil, Malory counsels his readers. The promise of fame and renown closes the old preface. A romance of 1860 takes that knightly frame for a tale of true love. Boston houses of that year fed a rich market in such tales. The publisher pair here also backed bold new writing of the age. Harrington stands as their bid in the romance trade.
58387-death-to-the-inquisitive-a-story-o:
Death to the Inquisitive, a story of sinful love, is a sensational novel by Lurana W Sheldon, printed at New York in 1892. Its motto warns the reader not to unmask man's heart and view the hell that is there. The frontispiece shows the scarlet house of sin. The contents open with the Whitechapel mystery and a suicidal attempt.

A shame-born child, a painful reminiscence, and the breath of passion follow. Maurice Sinclair escapes with his victim, and Julia Webber lays plans for revenge. Later chapters bring a deer hunt in Newfoundland, Stella restored to her lover, and Doctor Seward's experiment. Queen Liz, the marriage certificate, and a home in New York fill the later pages. Sam Lee discovers a faro game near the end. Sheldon's tale is a dime-novel melodrama of crime, passion, and revenge in the city.
58502-madame-x-a-story-of-mother-love:
McConaughy novelized Madame X from the play by Alexandre Bisson here. Grosset and Dunlap printed the mother love story in 1910. Volkert drew the plates for the tale of a woman of mystery. Table heads run two invalids, the return, and Magdalen first.

Defence and prosecution openings frame a trial at the book heart. The wanderers, a hotel of three crowns, and dower claims follow. A ghost rises, hope dawns, and Madame X speaks at trial. The verdict and a guttering flame close the twenty five chapters. A Massenet elegie on spring days long ago stands before chapter one in the book.
58711-traced-and-tracked-or-memoirs-of-a:
Traced and Tracked, or Memoirs of a City Detective, is a book by James McGovan of Edinburgh. It was printed there by John Menzies and Company in 1886, in its seventh edition. McGovan also wrote Brought to Bay, Hunted Down and Strange Clues. The four books together form the full set of his detective experiences. This volume is inscribed to John Leng of Newport in Fife, in thanks for kindness during a grave illness of the author.

In his preface of October 1884, McGovan says his former books had sold twenty five thousand copies, and the demand kept up. His works had been turned into German at Berlin and into French at Geneva. The contents open with a case called A Pedestrian's Plot. The book gives case after case from a city detective's working life.
58776-the-life-of-bismarck-private-and-p:
A biography of Otto von Bismarck by Johann Georg Ludwig Hesekiel. Harper and Brothers published the English edition at New York in 1870. Kenneth R H Mackenzie translated and edited it. His version adds an introduction, notes, and appendices. Upward of one hundred illustrations enrich the volume. With God for king and fatherland stands as its motto.

The first book traces the Bismarcks of olden time. Their name's origin on the river Biese opens the inquiry. Castellans at Burgstall castle carry the family through the middle ages. Claus von Bismarck rises into the margrave's council in the fourteenth century. Excommunication, guild politics, and Bohemian overlordship fill the chronicle. The life proper then follows Otto from ancestry to power.
59258-the-golden-slave:
The Golden Slave is an historical novel by Poul Anderson, issued at New York by the Avon Book Division in 1960 as an Avon original. Its hero is Eodan, a king of the Cimbri, made a slave. The scene in the head shows him brought before Cordelia, whose husband set a king to work in his fields. She pours wine for him and proposes a better understanding between them.

Anderson's author's note grounds the romance in the record. This might have happened, he writes. The Cimbri are still remembered by the old district name Himmerland in Jutland. Plutarch describes the battle at Vercellae of 101 BC and its aftermath. The novel threads its invented slave king through those real wars of Rome's northern frontier.
59760-the-detective-s-clew-or-the-traged:
The Detective's Clew, or The Tragedy of Elm Grove, is a dime novel by Old Hutch, printed by Street and Smith of New York. It ran as number 14 of the Secret Service Series, a monthly devoted to stories of the detection of crime. The December 1888 number sold by subscription at three dollars a year.

The plot follows Geoffrey Haywood through a brother's message, a fight and a flight, and an arrest. A wrong man is taken, then freed. A New York detective and a custom-house detective both work the case. Strange discoveries and a secret journey fill the middle chapters. A glad meeting ends the tale, in the brisk manner of the house.
60404-the-first-book-of-eve:
First Book of Eve is a comic picture book from the Tatler weekly. Brentano's of New York issued the book form in the year 1916. Drawings are by Fish, and the text and design are by Fowl. Eve's adventures ran each week in the Tatler before book form. That paper is billed as the brightest and most unique weekly in the world.

The book is dedicated to the boys in khaki and in blue. Letters from the North Sea, France, Africa, and Mesopotamia praised the sketches. Soldiers wrote that Eve brightened dull and gloomy hours at the front. Eve kept gay and frivolous on purpose, to please those men at war. Light froth with a wartime heart beats under the jokes and drawings.
60454-choyce-drollery-songs-and-sonnets-:
Woodfall Ebsworth edited a reprint of Choyce Drollery, a song and sonnet book of 1656, printed at Boston in Lincolnshire in 1876. Songs and sonnets of several eminent authors fill the old pages. The extra songs of Merry Drollery of 1661 and an Antidote Against Melancholy of the same year are added. Ebsworth gives special introductions and appendices of notes, illustrations, and text fixes.

His introduction tells how Choice Drollery was banned, and sets the two courts of 1656 side by side. Songs of love and war are sorted and weighed. Westminster Drolleries of 1674 add more songs at the back. Lovers of old English verse get a merry, bawdy, loyal book of the Restoration dawn, saved and explained by a keen editor.
60978-will-somers-the-boy-detective:
Will Somers, the Boy Detective is a dime novel by Charles Morris, issued as number 62 of Beadle's Pocket Library in March 1885. Beadle and Adams of New York published the weekly library at five cents a number. The opening chapter is called Looking for Work. Will Somers is a boy of some sixteen years, well built and athletic, his strong limbs showing through rents in his worn clothes.

His claim to good looks, the narrator says, is beyond dispute, with a bright black eye and dark curls over an olive face. He asks a gentleman, in bold slang, whether there is any opening in the place for a fellow of his size and looks. He is not particular, he drawls: most anything will do, say cashier. A line preserved in the copy shows his code as a detective.
61124-psychoanalysis-and-love:
Psychoanalysis and Love is a popular exposition of the new psychology of love by Andre Tridon, published in New York by Brentano's in 1922. Tridon belonged to medico-legal and forensic societies in New York and to the Vienna association for individual psychology. His credentials frame the book as expert counsel for lay readers.

The first chapter, The Head and the Heart, opens the argument. Love, Tridon holds, is independent of the will. His headings speak of victims of Venus and of love and affection as separate forces. The book applies psychoanalytic ideas about desire and the unconscious to courtship and marriage. Such volumes carried Freud's vocabulary into American parlours in the twenties. Tridon writes as an interpreter, turning clinical theory into guidance for the lovelorn and the married alike.
6116-out-of-the-primitive:
Robert Ames Bennet opens Out of the Primitive with castaways north of the Zambezi, where a little tramp rescue steamer runs miles into the offing and lays to through dark hours. Coral reefs fringing Africa's southeast coast make moonless nights decidedly undesirable for such a vessel.

The Earl of Avondale steps from a close, hot stateroom into coolness before dawn, reads the Southern Cross to port, and knows the steamer heads for the coast. Phosphorescent light crinkles the black sea under a faint breeze heavy with rotting vegetation. Bennet sets a tale of rank, wreck, and wilderness survival.
61174-dick-merriwell-s-day-or-iron-nerve:
Dick Merriwell Day stands in the long Merriwell set of tales for young men. The fifteen cent tales star Frank and Dick Merriwell as hero brothers. Front pages praise the set for sports thrills and clean moral tone. Half a million fans were said to follow the brothers tales.

The set was pitched to fire a boy aim to be a strong athlete. Tales span school days, Yale, races, and trips west and south. Iron nerve is the theme the title gives this volume. Readers get sport, grit, and fair play in the Merriwell mold throughout.
62274-the-stranger-in-shrewsbury-or-an-h:
The Stranger in Shrewsbury is a guide to the town of Shrewsbury and its surroundings by Thomas Howell. This text is the second edition, printed and sold by the author in 1824. Howell's preface thanks his fellow townsmen for the friendly patronage given to the first edition. The title page quotes verse praising the spot as home.

Such stranger's guides walked a visitor through a town's history, buildings, and walks. Howell's book mixes history with description of the town on the Severn and the country round it. It served travellers in the coaching age who wanted a town explained in a small compass. The careless old spelling of the history section is kept in this copy.
62503-summer-of-love:
Summer of Love is a book of poems by Joyce Kilmer. The Baker and Taylor Company published it in New York in 1911. Kilmer dedicated the volume to Aline, his wife. A dedication poem casts him as a vagrant minstrel. He lays his book of verses at her feet.

The contents list some eighty poems. Love songs lead the collection. Titles include a villanelle of Loveland and a ballade of butterflies. Other poems treat a book-shop, a subway, and Madison Square grass. One poem honours Florence Nightingale in memoriam. Another imitates a ballade by Richepin. The title poem opens the book. It praises June for lavishing sweetness on everything. Even the leaves, Kilmer writes, grow drunk with bliss.
62698-the-golden-boys-on-the-river-drive:
The Golden Boys on the River Drive is a boys' adventure novel by Wyman, dean of the Pennsylvania Military College. The Burt Company of New York published it in 1923. It belongs to a series written for boys of twelve to sixteen. Other volumes send the same heroes into the Maine woods and to a fortress.

The story opens on Moosehead Lake in northern Maine as the ice breaks. Bob Golden, nineteen, stands on a wharf with his brother Jack, a year younger. Both are tall, strong, and shaped by years in the open air. Their home is Skowhegan, some fifty miles to the south of the lake. They are cadets at a military college in Pennsylvania, home on vacation.
63532-within-a-budding-grove:
Within a Budding Grove is a novel by Marcel Proust, in Scott Moncrieff's English version, printed at New York. The Modern Library issued it, under a copyright of 1924. The translator's dedication, dated at Bad Kissingen on July 31, 1923, is a poem to a dead friend. It speaks of friends garnered in the cold granaries of death.

Part one, Madame Swann at Home, brings old friends in new aspects: the Marquis de Norpois, Bergotte, and a parting from Gilberte. Place-names follow, with the narrator's first visit to Balbec. Part two introduces Charlus and Robert de Saint-Loup, dinners at Rivebelle, and Albertine among a frieze of girls. The novel opens with a family debate over guests.
63617-the-ultimate-eve:
The Ultimate Eve is a science fiction story by H Sanford Effron, first printed in Planet Stories in the winter of 1954. A ship settles to the ground in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains on an April morning in 1955. The landing goes unobserved. The world faces too many crises of its own making to watch for an invasion from space.

A man steps from the lock and studies the landscape. His features and body are human, though he is too well muscled and his face unusually handsome. He is glad to have landed so near the cabin chosen as his goal. The place is well isolated, a good testing ground for the weapon. Even the scientists of this planet, he reflects, used animal life to test their puny weapons. Now man himself would be the guinea pig.
6373-the-luck-of-roaring-camp-and-other-:
Bret Harte's volume gathers the Luck of Roaring Camp and other tales with condensed novels, Spanish and American legends, and earlier papers, introduced by the author. In 1882 his scattered work was brought into five compact volumes, and in 1897 his publishers undertook a uniform presentation of more than thirty years of poems, tales, sketches, and romances. This book samples that long output in one place.

A bright October day in the California Sierras opens one tale, with a sylvan lake, an Indian village's smoke among lofty pines, and Judge Tompkins's log cottage among buckeyes. Inside, goldfish in an aquarium and a grand piano show cultivation within a humble exterior, while paintings from Van Dyke to Turner hang on the walls. Harte writes the west with irony and tenderness, where rough camps hold refined hearts.
63791-for-a-night-of-love:
For a Night of Love is a tale by Emile Zola, in an English form put out at New York in the early nineteen hundreds. It opens on a small town built on a hill, its name cut to a first mark in the text. At the foot of its old walls runs a deep brook with a song name.

A stone bridge of one arch, on the road from a great town, spans that brook at the south gate. Its broad low walls serve as seats for the old folk of the edge of town. Past it a street climbs to a still square paved with huge stones, where weed grows thick as in a field. The houses sleep, and a dogs bark at a rare foot step is the towns sole stir.
64759-the-last-two-alive:
Alfred Coppel wrote The Last Two Alive, a science fiction tale printed in the November 1950 issue of Planet Stories. Aram Jerrold has rebelled against the Tetrarchy, the government of the Thirty Suns, and waits in a dark courtroom for the verdict of death. The Supreme Council itself will demand it. He has been badgered, beaten, drugged, and questioned for weeks, shunted from bureau to bureau, and rung dry.

Above his dread runs a command from the past: you must save something from the ruins. Santane's beast-rockets have screamed into the void bearing madness to the Thirty Suns, and space war threatens to smash galactic civilization for good. Coppel sets one broken rebel against the end of a star-spanning order. The tale asks what one man, marked for death, can still keep alive when all else falls.
64856-the-fireless-locomotive:
Dayton, Ohio supplies the scene for this account of three fireless locomotives bought by the National Cash Register Company. Fireless engines carry no fire of their own. They run on steam stored in a large tank, which made them safe and handy for switching work in a factory yard. The three engines, nicknamed the Three Little Engines, were the Rubicon, the Dayton, and the South Park.

The book centers on the Rubicon, which arrived in nineteen nine on a flat car. It worked until a modern Diesel switcher replaced it. In the summer of nineteen sixty two the old engine was refurbished for display at Carillon Park. On one of its last trips it pushed its own replacement across the yard to the engine house. Photographs mark each stage of the handover. The result is a small, affectionate piece of industrial history.
65777-treve:
Treve is a dog novel by Albert Payson Terhune of Sunnybank. Grosset and Dunlap issued it in New York, with rights from 1924. Terhune also wrote Lad: A Dog, Bruce, Buff, and Gray Dawn. He dedicates Treve to Ellen Comly, Treve's friend and his own. Nine chapters run from The Coming of Treve to his later trials.

Thirst, a marooning, and a killer fill the early chapter heads. A secret adventure, desertion, and theft and untheft vary the dog's fortunes. In the hands of the enemy and a matinee close the contents list. Collie heart and courage carry the tale, as in all Terhune books. Dog lovers of the twenties prized his true, unsentimental kennel eye.
6616-december-love:
Robert Hichens opens in a London club, where Francis Braybrooke, a man who knows everybody, sits down beside Alick Craven of the Foreign Office. Braybrooke loves people, not ideas, and cannot live away from the center of human doings; new faces are his delight. Craven, back from war service, listens as talk turns to love late in life.

December Love, as its title hints, weighs passion that comes when youth has passed, with all its grace and risk. Hichens writes with a social novelist's eye for talk, manners, and the small shifts of feeling. The novel is a polished, adult romance of London life, where age does not end desire.
66313-journey-for-the-brave:
Journey for the Brave is a science fiction tale by Alan Nourse, first printed in Imagination in April 1954. Its blurb sets the theme: courage will be a chief need for the pilot of the first moon rocket. But who decides if a man is brave, or a coward? The hero is Scotty Johnson, a wiry man of five foot two. The tale opens in a hot base diner in New Mexico. His friends Mitch and Jack have slipped him out of town ahead of the press.

They drink a last coffee in tense quiet, and watch him as if to keep him there. Scotty is vexed to be the calm one while the shore crew shakes. A jeep screeches up outside, and a military police driver calls him out. The ride to the rocket strip begins. The tale builds its test of nerve in the hours before Zero Hour.
66376-young-musgrave:
Mrs Oliphant wrote the novel Young Musgrave. Macmillan and Company issued this form at London in 1894. Three volumes held its first form in 1877. One volume held the second in 1878. Globe and crown reprints kept it in print. A motto from old Franciscan sermons heads it. Give all, even to the spoiling of thy goods, it urges.

No man can redeem his brother, a psalm adds below. Part One opens with The Family chapter. Mary and The New-Comers follow in that part. After the Silence of Years opens Part Two. Waking Up and At the Vicarage fill it. The Children at the Castle start Part Three. Lady Stanton and Elf Dale stand in that part. A tale of sacrifice and a young man's burden, the novel tests its stern motto against family love.
66503-with-sword-and-crucifix-being-an-a:
Edward Van Zile set this romance on La Salle's road to the Mississippi in 1682. Harper printed With Sword and Crucifix at New York and London in 1900. Its hero, Count Louis de Sancerre, rides as the great explorer's companion.

The sword and the crucifix, whispers De Sancerre in the front plate, pointing to the soldier and the priest. A great explorer listens at midnight to a tale of love in the first chapter. A mystery confronts the count in the next, and a maiden shows her heart. La Salle reaches a fateful choice, and Juan Rodriquez takes his revenge. Satan has his way with the Concepcion, and the cross is carried to a city of idolaters.
6670-christmas-eve:
Robert Browning's Christmas Eve bursts out of a little chapel into fresh night air, after rain drove in gusts down the common. The speaker waited five minutes in the doorway, then squeezed past fumbling hands at the inner door, into a sheepfold entry six feet long by three feet wide. He blocked half of it, eyed like a wild beast by the flock within.

From that cramped, comic start, the poem moves into a wide vision of faith, doubt, and Christmas night. Browning's verse is dense, vivid, and full of sudden turns. Christmas Eve is a great, strange poem, where a rainy chapel visit opens onto questions of belief itself.
67186-the-rider-of-the-mohave:
James Fellom wrote a western story printed at New York in 1924. The book is given to those who, having paid the penalty for their misdeeds, seek to regain their places among the law abiding. He rides by night, says the prologue. Mania and dreams and the man hunter open the chapters. In which wills collide and Lemuel yields follow.

The wherewithal, aftermath, and startling predicaments fill the middle. Lavender and old lace, evidence to convict, and a disclosure raise the stakes. The hand of Quintell, one silent night, and skulking shadows lead on. An enemy in the ranks, Geerusalem stirs, and the law and the lawless close the tale. An ex outlaw rides for a second chance in the desert country.
67376-that-s-not-love:
That's Not Love, by Elisabeth Sanxay Holding, opens at Serena Page's country place, billed in its heading as a house of mirth where merriment and tragedy are often close together. A gay world greets the summer morning: the sprinkler flings a rainbow mist, diamonds shine on the grass blades, and curtains flutter at the open windows.

Serena has arisen at half past eight, an outrageous hour for her guests, and her rising somehow disturbs the whole house. Creating an exciting bustle about her, without doing anything herself, is her especial talent. She comes down in a filmy black negligee, her handsome, haggard face pale without make-up. In the breakfast room waits Geraldine Moriarty, whose enigmatic smile is getting on Serena's nerves. Serena longs for an excuse to fly into a rage, her only way of getting rid of people.
68625-the-red-wizard-or-the-cave-captive:
Lieutenant Ned Hunter wrote The Red Wizard, a dime tale put out in New York by Beadle and Adams. Rights were held from 1872 by Frank Starr and his firm. The tale opens in the wild west, with a threat made at white heat. A man warns a foe not to strike a young Native girl.

Wash Lawton, a scout, makes the threat and stands by it with force. He says cold blood slaying is not his way, though he does his share in a fair fight. A third man backs him and calls such slaying a shame on all men. Parsons backs down, but warns that the girl has eyes, ears, and feet to bear news. The spat sets up the tale of a cave captive, a red chief, and fights on the edge of the wilds.
68697-toying-with-fate-or-nick-carter-s-:
Nicholas Carter wrote Toying with Fate, or Nick Carter's Narrow Shave, for Street and Smith of New York. The firm copyrighted the dime novel in 1903. Carter's adventures ran in the New Magnet Library alone. The publisher calls them among the best detective tales ever written.

Front pages puff the publisher's whole list. Paper-covered novels are sorted for men, women, and boys. Adventure, love, society, and mystery all have their shelves. The story itself opens with a warning about libraries. Most people think a public library a fine thing, the narrator says. Few think of the great risk run by anyone who takes a book out. From that unlikely danger the detective story grows.
68950-twenty-three-and-a-half-hours-leav:
Twenty Three and a Half Hours' Leave is a story by Mary Roberts Rinehart, published in New York in nineteen eighteen. Illustrations by May Wilson Preston appear in the book, with a frontispiece set in an elevator. In that scene a woman tells a soldier, out of a clear sky, that he will have to take his raincoat off. Rinehart's tales of Bab and The Amazing Interlude are listed as her kin works.

A soldier's brief leave from camp in the Great War gives the tale its clock. Romance and comedy must fit inside twenty three and a half hours, no more. Rinehart mixes mystery habits with light love in her best selling manner. The raincoat order promises the flirtatious mix at once.
69372-narrative-of-henry-watson-a-fugiti:
Narrative of Henry Watson, a Fugitive Slave, was written by himself and published at Boston in eighteen forty eight. A dedication to a Mr Henry Holt opens the book. Watson thanks him for kind and humane interference on his behalf when he was a helpless slave, he writes. Without that help the little narrative would never have been published, he says.

I was born in Virginia, about thirteen miles from Fredericksburg, he begins. His mother was a slave belonging to a man named Bibb, he says. She was called Letty, for slaves seldom have but one name. He was called Bill as a child. He never had any brother or sister that he knows of, he adds. Slaves keep the births of their children by the seasons of the year, he explains.
69478-the-girls-of-rivercliff-school-or-:
The Girls of Rivercliff School, published in 1916, is Amy Bell Marlowe's school story of Beth Baldwin. Grosset and Dunlap sold the volume at sixty cents, with the rest of Marlowe's girl books. Mary Devine, whose ruling passion is news, chases Beth down the street on a hot day. She clings to her friend's arm, panting, with something to tell.

Thirty chapters carry Beth through her school year. Great-grandmother Lomis's corals, a sacrifice and an adventure in midstream come early. A red masque, a traitor's blow and a hearing before the judgment seat raise the stakes. An ice carnival and a final chapter on vocations round out the year. Beth's resolve, named in the subtitle, holds through it all.
69510-goa-and-the-blue-mountains-or-six-:
Richard Burton wrote Goa and the Blue Mountains in 1851. Six months of sick leave is the book's second title. Bentley at London put it out that year for him. Burton was a lieutenant in the Bombay army then. Coonoor fronts the book as its plate.

The Voyage opens the contents of the Indian journey. New Goa and Old Goa as it was follow in the chapters. Old Goa as it is and a return to Panjim come next. Panjim's population and Seroda take chapters. Education, professions, and oriental studies stand in the list. Adieu to Panjim, Calicut, and Malabar follow in order. The Hindus and Moslems of Malabar take chapters of their own. A land journey and a first glimpse of Ooty close the contents. Burton gives India a sick officer's sharp-eyed holiday.
69858-motherly-talks-with-young-housekee:
Motherly Talks with Young Housekeepers is a household guide by Mrs Beecher. Ford issued it in New York in 1873. It holds eighty-seven brief articles on home topics. About five hundred cooking receipts follow the talks. The pieces first ran in The Christian Union. Readers asked for them so often that a book was made. The publishers call it a friendly monitor for young wives.

Beecher holds that home is woman's chief place of work. System in work opens the talks. Months, seasons, and duties are taken in turn. The receipts are vouched for by her own testing. Such books trained new housekeepers in a strict age. They joined moral counsel to kitchen craft. Beecher was a sister of Harriet Beecher Stowe. Her voice carries the same earnest, kindly tone. The volume is a mine of period housekeeping.
70723-drugs-that-enslave:
Doctor Kane of New York wrote Drugs That Enslave, on the opium, morphine, chloral, and hashisch habits, published by Presley Blakiston at Philadelphia in 1881. The preface says the book grew from letters by physicians at home and abroad. They asked about the signs, outlook, and treatment of the habits, and found the plain facts hard to come by. Kane drew on his own observation, the literature, and nearly a thousand correspondents worldwide. Little space goes to hashisch, rare in this country.

The frontispiece is the Laocoon, straining at his knotted coils, and the text opens with Coleridge's plea that his wretchedness be published as a warning. Kane names Coleridge, De Quincey, and other famous sufferers, then gives statistics on the fast growth of opium and morphine use in the United States. The book is dedicated to his old teacher, the Brooklyn surgeon Alexander Skene.
70877-the-mystery-at-lovers-cave:
Anthony Berkeley wrote a detective novel round his amateur sleuth Roger Sheringham. Roger takes a third piece of toast and teases his cousin Anthony at breakfast. Anthony had failed to learn their train from Saint Pancras before the trip. A telephone and an enquiry office existed, Anthony retorts, and the sparring sets the tone.

Inspector Moresby joins the case with reluctance. Chapters promise girls and murder, a goat faced clergyman, real bad blood, and a midnight expedition. A shoe is found, an arrest is prepared, and a scoundrel meets his end. Poisons and pipes, caustic soda, and Colin upsetting the apple cart fill a brisk puzzle that Roger solves at last.
70924-the-adventures-of-dora-bell-detect:
The Adventures of Dora Bell, Detective is a set of twelve stories by Elizabeth Burgoyne Corbett. They first ran in the South Wales Echo in 1894, in weekly parts. Papers in Britain, America, and Australia picked the series up again. The first story opens with a client begging for secret help. His property has passed into other hands, and ruin waits if the news spreads. The police, he insists, must know nothing of it.

His customers would flee if they suspected their plate and jewels were gone. A gay season, he argues, keeps society dames content to leave valuables pledged. Story titles promise a sweep, a broken trust, and a mysterious thief. One story is frankly called One of Dora's Failures. The Recluse of Hallow Hall and Miss Rankin's Rival fill out the set. Dora Bell stands among the earliest women detectives in fiction.
70936-the-wizard-s-cave:
The Wizard's Cave is a boys' adventure story by Eglanton Thorne. The Religious Tract Society of London published it. Two brothers, Duke and Noel Bryden, open the tale. Duke is a well grown boy of twelve; Noel is younger and slighter. On breaking up day they watch their schoolmates leave for home. The brothers have no home to go to, so the holidays must pass at school.

Rain keeps them in the grim empty schoolroom at Tudor Hall. Their talk turns to a past summer at Deal by the sea. The contents promise a wreckers' lamp and a cave to explore. An old house hides an amazing discovery. Duke's Beacon and the mystery of the cave carry the middle chapters. Noel guards the secret, and the last chapter is called No Coward After All. The tale suits young readers who like coast and mystery.
71088-the-chemical-nature-of-the-alpha-p:
Ernest Rutherford gave his Nobel talk on what alpha sparks are made of. The talk was made on December 11, 1908. Alpha rays' traits had played a great part in rays' lore, he starts. Much of all ray work hangs on the shot alpha bits, he holds. His talk gives a brief past of what men had learned of them.

Alpha rays were first seen as a kind of their own in 1899. Six years of hard tests then chased one tough ask in full. What stuff are the alpha bits in their true chemic kind. Long and hard was the test path to that solve, he says. Bench men of that age get a chief's own tale of the hunt. Each step is told plain.
71220-report-of-the-naval-committee-to-t:
The Naval Committee reported to the House of Representatives in August 1850 in favor of a line of mail steamships to the western coast of Africa. The line would run thence via the Mediterranean to London. It was designed to promote the emigration of free persons of color from the United States to Liberia. It would also increase the steam navy and extend the commerce of the United States.

An appendix was added by the American Colonization Society. The memorial of Judge Bryan was referred to the Committee on Naval Affairs, the report says. Its members are named by state: Stanton of Tennessee, Bocock of Virginia, Schenck of Ohio, and Gerry of Maine among them. The proposition extends a system recently commenced by Congress: a powerful steam navy, to be used in time of peace in carrying the mails. Colonization and sea power sail in one bill here.
73308-love:
Love is a novel by the author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden. Macmillan published it in London in 1925. The author is not named on the title page. Part one opens at a performance of The Immortal Hour. That play was running to almost empty houses at King's Cross. The first meeting of Christopher and Catherine happens there unknowingly. They went so often that regulars knew each other by sight. She first notices him on her fifth visit, the narrator says.

Two people behind her boast of their attendance before the curtain. One is proud of an eleventh visit to the play. The other answers carelessly that this is his thirty second. She turns, amused, and sees Christopher consciously for the first time. He sees her in the same moment across the thin audience. A theatre devotion becomes the path into love.
73660-the-robbers-cave:
The Robbers' Cave: A Tale of Italy is a children's adventure novel signed with the pen name A L O E, printed here by the Bible Institute Colportage Association of Chicago. The contents list eighteen chapters, from a Calabrian inn to the robbers' cave and victory.

The story opens on a carriage crossing Calabria in suffocating heat. Young Horace Cleveland, spoiled and imperious, abuses the driver and scorns his tired mother's wish that they had stayed in comfortable Naples. Horace is drunk on scenery and on his own importance, certain he is superior to everyone he meets in Italy. His mother sighs over the whim that dragged her into this wild land. The contrast between the vain son and the weary mother, set in bandit country, frames a moral adventure for young readers.
73782-what-i-believe:
Bertrand Russell set out his own creed in a short book of the To-day and To-morrow line. The series dealt with science and the years to come. Haldane and Schiller wrote books in the same small line. Russell's book is named in that list as What I Believe. Its form is brief by the plan of the whole line.

In few pages, a great mind states what he holds true. Such books asked big asks in small compass for home readers. Russell writes on faith, doubt, and how men should live. His prose stays clear, calm, and blunt at once. Thinkers of 1925 took these small books up with zeal.
73929-danny-the-detective:
Danny the Detective is a boys crime tale by Barclay, with pictures through the text. It came out at New York and London in the last years of the great war, and its rights were set in law that year. A front print shows an evil face at a hole in a wall, close behind its hero.

Its parts run like a case book of the war years. A straw loft, a strange man, a mill pond, and the dark hours of one night open the hunt. Then come a dark hall, spies, a white face in moon light, and a wire tapped in secret. Free, in the hands of the scouts, caught at last, and a well done close the case. The form is plain: a lad cracks a spy plot in his own town.
740-remarks-of-mr-calhoun-of-south-carol:
John C. Calhoun spoke in the Senate on 15 February 1833 on nullification and the Force Bill, at the height of the clash over tariffs. South Carolina had claimed the right to void federal law, and Congress debated a bill to enforce it by force. Calhoun rose to defend his state and to press the limits of federal power.

His speech opens on the public debt, declared all but paid, and on the hopes that died with a long, fruitless session. From there he argues the case for state rights against coercion. The text is a key source for the nullification crisis, showing Calhoun's logic at its sharpest and the temper of a Union under strain.
74313-the-merry-five:
The Merry Five is a children's story by Penn Shirley, author of the Little Miss Weezy books. It belongs to the Silver Gate series, published in Boston by Lee and Shepard in 1896. Each volume of the series sold for seventy-five cents. A frontispiece caption reads: Mamma has found her lost baby.

Chapters follow the five children through a year of play: Donald hides, they learn to swim, and they go to the beach. They fish for Weezy, camp out, and turn little miners. A bee ranch, five young poets, and a street masquerade fill later chapters. Molly plays the heroine in one tale. The book is a cheerful record of childhood summers of its time.
74968-poems-of-love:
Poems of Love is a verse collection by Ella Wheeler Wilcox, published at Chicago with copyright in nineteen hundred five. Wilcox lists her earlier books, Poems of Passion, Poems of Pleasure, and Poems of Reflection, on the title page. A long contents list names dozens of short love poems. Sweet Danger and A Fatal Impress stand at its head.

Love I Will Be True, The Kingdom of Love, and Love Will Wane show the range of her themes. Faithful love, parting, loss, and a baby in the house all get a poem. Wilcox was famed for verse that spoke plain feeling in rhymed lines for a mass readership. Heart over craft is the bargain her readers sought.
75237-there-was-once-a-slave:
Shirley Graham wrote There Was Once a Slave, the heroic story of Frederick Douglass, published by Julian Messner in New York in 1947. The book won the sixty-five hundred dollar Julian Messner Award for the best book combating intolerance in America. Judges Carl Van Doren, Lewis Gannett, and Clifton Fadiman chose it from over six hundred manuscripts.

Graham tells Douglass's life in three parts called the Road, the Lightning, and the Storm. Chapters follow the enslaved boy around Chesapeake Bay, through his work in Washington, and across the Atlantic. The story covers his escape, his speeches, and his fight against slavery. Written for general readers, the biography presents Douglass as a hero whose rise from bondage carried a lesson for a country still marked by racial injustice.
75463-red-love:
Alexandra Kollontay wrote a novel of love and new morals in Soviet Russia. Seven Arts Publishing Company issued Red Love in New York in 1927. Two printings ran in March of that year alone. A front note calls the book a study of sex ties after the war.

Kollontay holds that working women must now be judged as citizens, not wives alone. Family duty and public work clash hard in the new woman's life, she argues. Her Russian scene stands for a change felt across all lands, she writes. Readers gain a famed, bold novel from a voice of the revolution.
76287-the-despot-of-broomsedge-cove:
The Despot of Broomsedge Cove is a novel by Charles Egbert Craddock, held under an 1888 copyright and printed at Boston in 1889. Craddock was the pen name of Mary N Murfree. She had written In the Tennessee Mountains and The Prophet of the Great Smoky Mountains.

The tale opens on a steep, wild slope of the Great Smoky Mountains, where the old forest runs unbroken for miles. One thin clearing and one log cabin, high on the rugged slant, mark man presence. At night the stars seem no more aloof than the valley below. By day the mountains press in with solemn nearness. One day a sound cuts the silence, faint and far, with no kin to wood, water, beast, or bird. Mountain tale fans get Murfree moody art at its best.
76379-catechism-of-the-locomotive:
Forney, a mechanical engineer, wrote a plain guide to the locomotive in question and answer form. The Railroad Gazette entered the book in 1874. Plates near the front show a side cut and a plan of an American engine by the Grant works of Paterson, New Jersey. The book sold by mail at two dollars and a half.

In his preface Forney tells how the work began. His paper had a German book on the same plan turned into English, and asked him to fit it to American practice. He found that the German book covered but a small part of the ground he had marked out. So he wrote a new book in its place, owing the idea and some matter to Kosak. Other books on heat and steam are named among his sources. It is a starter's handbook for engine men of that day.
77040-le-selve:
Ouida wrote this tale, printed at London in 1896. The first scene is set at night in the wilds of Italy, as the name of the book says in that tongue. It was a cold black night, with no moon and no stars. An old man of the soil lay at the point of death. He was all on his own. No one thought it worth the loss of time to sit by him.

He was eighty-three years old, and in the eyes of his sons he ought to have been dead long in front of this fall of the year. They and their kin sat round a fire of logs and chips, and talked twixt them. They did not talk of him; he was no more of any weight in their minds.
77835-a-cowboy-detective:
Chas. A. Siringo wrote this true tale of his own life, printed in 1912. A photo at its front shows the author as he stood past the riots at Coeur d'Alene. A next plate shows his old Colt gun of six shots, and the hand that kept it in check. The full head of the book gives its span. It is two and a score of years with a world-famed house of sleuths. It gives the inside facts of the wild fights of work at Coeur d'Alene as well.

The list of parts fills the pledge. His first work was at the riot of the foes of all rule at Chicago. There he sat in jail for the slug of a slugger.
78210-dorcas-dene-detective:
George Sims wrote these adventures of Dorcas Dene, a woman detective, in a second series of nine stories narrated by her friend Saxon. The titles run from The Missing Prince and The Morganatic Wife to The House in Regent's Park, The Handkerchief Sachet, and The One Who Knew. A bank holiday mystery and a piece of brown paper supply two more cases.

The Missing Prince opens at the Alhambra theatre, where the manager frets because a royal box stands empty. A foreign prince, heir to a throne, has not arrived, and the ballet cannot wait. Saxon is pulled aside by a detective inspector and taken to supper at the Cavour, where Dorcas explains her interest.
