She had come to see whether the prince would occupy his box, and she and Inspector Carr are already trying to fathom why he has vanished.
78848-jim-hanvey-detective:
Octavus Roy Cohen wrote Jim Hanvey, Detective, issued at New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1923. Cohen had written The Crimson Alibi and Midnight before it. Seven tales make up the book, among them Fish Eyes, Homespun Silk, Common Stock, and Caveat Emptor, each a case for the detective whose name fronts the volume.

The first tale opens in the Third National Bank, where paying teller Clifford Wallace works ill at ease in his cage. More than a million and a quarter dollars in cash sits with him on the busiest day of the month, when the pay rolls of three large firms fall due. Cohen sets the money, the worry, and the white lock in Wallace's hair before Hanvey ever steps in.
7890-blind-love:
Wilkie Collins's Blind Love, completed by Walter Besant, runs through three periods of mounting intrigue. The first brings sour French wine, a man refused, a registered packet, and Mountjoy's game, lost, replayed, and won, beside a doctor doctored and a father's message.

Later Iris moves between home, Hampstead Heath, London, and Paris, through a lady's maid, a keyhole, a hospital mystery, and a school for husbands. Lord Harry's honeymoon, a decree of fate, and my lord's and my lady's minds close a tale of love, drink, and deceit, finished after Collins's death.
7891-the-dead-alive:
Wilkie Collins's The Dead Alive opens in a barrister's chambers in the Temple. A doctor tells Philip Lefrank his heart and lungs are sound: his disease is overwork, his remedy rest. Lefrank, a junior barrister from Jersey, faints at his desk and fears ruin if he stops, with briefs piled high in term time.

The tale that follows turns on a sick man, a supposed death, and a mystery of identity. Collins tells it with a knack for legal detail and surprise. Through courts, illness, and a life hung in doubt, the short novel asks who is truly dead, and what proof can bring a lost man back.
79140-the-trough-of-the-wave:
The Trough of the Wave is book one of The People of Juvik by Olav Duun of Norway. Arthur Chater turned the work to English from the tongue of its birth. The Norse book came out in nineteen twenty seven, the English in nineteen thirty. Six books in all trace the Juvik kin through four spans of life. A front note sets the scene in Namdal, north of Trondhjem, the man birth shire.

No lord class or great land house stands in that Norway, the note says. Free hold farm folk, whose land drops from sire to son, bear the old ways. Small croft men rent from them and serve as hired hands in lean years. Old Per Anders, last of the old sort, dies as new mills rise. His sons sink for a time in the trough of the wave.
79494-alick-s-cave:
Catharine Shaw wrote Alick Cave, or On the Cliff, a sequel to Alick Hero, in a new edition from John F Shaw and Company in London. Shaw had earlier written Something for Sunday and edited Sunday Sunshine. Twenty chapters fill the tale. Chapter one is Salome. A plate shows Margaret stealing in to sit close by her mother knee, listening. A Beatitudes line heads the chapter, Blessed are the poor in spirit.

Salome, a servant, talks with Master Charlie in coast dialect as the tale opens. Salome, has mother told you about Lionel and Marian, he asks. Nothing as I know of, dearie, she answers. Then I shall tell you the news, Charlie bursts forth, colouring with importance. A Shadow, On the Surface, and In the Cave follow. Salome Slate, Marian Sunshine, and Margaret Legacy fill the middle. Sunday school readers get a cliff village tale of children and faith.
7971-the-fugitive:
Rabindranath Tagore's The Fugitive, dedicated to W. W. Pearson, gathers dramatic poems and translations in three parts. The first pairs Kacha and Devayani, the second Ama and Vinayaka with a mother's prayer, and the third Somaka and Ritvik with Karna and Kunti. The opening lines address an eternal fugitive whose rushing steps sweep the dust of the world into sweetness and shake a sacred shower of death over life.

The pieces draw on Indian legend and myth, retold in Tagore's lyrical English. They are best read aloud or slowly, for their music and imagery carry much of their meaning. For readers coming to Tagore through his poems, this volume shows his dramatic imagination at work, and his habit of finding spiritual questions inside old stories.
8073-a-fool-for-love:
Francis Lynde, author of The Grafters and The Master of Appleby, wrote this railroad romance opening on a December morning in Kansas City. The Chicago and Alton's fast train, dripping from a rush through the wet night, steams into Union Station, and the chapters that follow move through switched engines. Changed itineraries, crystalline altitudes, a landslide, a rajah's order, the majesty of the law, block signals, spiked switches, and the right of way.

The novel mixes adventure with love, using the railroad as both setting and plot engine: schedules, signals, and wrecks decide fates. Lynde knew railroad life well, and his technical detail gives the romance ballast. For readers who enjoy early twentieth-century adventure fiction, it is a fast, vivid ride.
8076-the-history-of-david-grieve:
Mrs Humphry Ward, author of Robert Elsmere, told the history of David Grieve in four books: childhood, youth, storm and stress, and maturity. The novel opens in dialect, with David and his sister Louie on the steps of a house, a battered hat, and a tall, bony woman insisting the hat be tied on. From that northern childhood, David grows through work, love, and religious doubt toward a hard-won adult life.

Ward writes a Victorian novel of formation, attentive to class, industry, and faith in a changing England. David's story is long and serious, in the tradition of the bildungsroman, and it was widely read in its day. For readers of George Eliot and Thomas Hardy, it offers a comparable, if less famous, study of a young life shaped by place and conscience.
8664-the-glory-of-the-conquered-the-stor:
Susan Glaspell published this 1909 novel, dedicated to Dr A. L. Hageboeck, who made the book possible, as the story of a great love tested by illness and ambition. Part one follows Ernestine, a painter, and Karl, a scientist, through letters, homecomings, studio and laboratory, and a verdict that darkens their future. Science, art, and love are set against one another, and a warning and a premonition hang over the closing chapters.

Part two carries the couple into the consequences, where love must survive not triumph but loss and change. Glaspell, later a Pulitzer-winning playwright, writes with psychological care about a woman artist and a man of science. The glory of the conquered, the title suggests, lies in enduring rather than winning. Readers will find a serious early feminist novel, more interested in inner life than in plot fireworks.
9247-fragments-from-the-journal-of-a-sol:
Hawthorne's fragments from a solitary man's journal open with his poor friend Oberon, now asleep with the silent ages. Oberon died calmly of lung disease, his life ebbing like a tide, not flickering like a wasted lamp. His last words asked his friend to burn his papers, fearing some might be betrayed into print.

The old disconnected journal in the narrator's hands survived that plea, and these fragments come from it. They read as notes of a lonely mind, musing on life, death, and art. The piece remains a haunting scrap from Hawthorne's workshop, intimate and unfinished by design.
93-tom-sawyer-detective:
Tom Sawyer turns detective when a diamond robbery ends in murder on his uncle's farm. Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer, Detective sends Tom and Huck to Arkansas, where Uncle Silas stands accused. Twain notes the plot comes from a real Swedish criminal trial.

Three sleepers, a ghostly talk, and the finding of Jupiter Dunlap build the case. Tom spots the flaw in the prosecution and names the true killers. The accused confesses in public, as in the source trial. The short novel mixes frontier humor with a fair-play mystery. The mystery's fairness, with clues laid plain, pleased readers who love to solve alongside Tom.
9603-hung-lou-meng-or-the-dream-of-the-r:
Book one of Hung Lou Meng, or The Dream of the Red Chamber, opens Cao Xueqin's great Chinese novel in H. Bencraft Joly's translation. Joly, a British consular man in China, began the work as a student in Peking, puzzled by the novel's maze. His preface, dated Macao, September 1891, owns faults in prose and rhyme, but hopes to aid students of Chinese. The tale opens with Chen Shih-yin in a vision.

Chia Yü-ts'un enters a dusty world of fate, dreams, and great houses, as the Jia family's fortunes unfold. Verse, dreams, and household intrigue mix from the first chapter. A reader gets the gateway to one of the world's great novels, in a pioneer's English version.
9604-hung-lou-meng-or-the-dream-of-the-r:
Book two of Hung Lou Meng, or The Dream of the Red Chamber, continues Cao Xueqin's great Chinese novel, here in H. Bencraft Joly's translation. Chapter twenty-five opens with dark arts at work on Pao-yü and Lady Feng, who meet five devils. The gem of spiritual perception, in a fit of torpor, meets two perfect men. Hsiao Hung's troubled dream of Chia Yün sets the chapter's eerie tone.

Later scenes follow the great Jia household through love, spite, and fate, as dreams blur with waking life. Joly's version brings Qing dynasty manners, verse, and intrigue to English readers. A reader gets a further stretch of one of the world's great novels, rich in family drama and Buddhist-Taoist wonder.
a-bit-o-love:
John Galsworthy sets his play in a village of the West of England, with the action passing on Ascension Day, as the scene list states. The persons include Michael Strangway, a curate with strange, tender ideas, his wife Beatrice, and the farmers and laborers of the parish: Burlacombes, Trustafords, Jarlands, and Freemans. Strangway's charity toward a thief has set the village against him.

Three acts move between Strangway's rooms, the village inn, the churchyard, and a barn. His wife has left him for another man, and the parish wants a harder, more respectable priest. Galsworthy writes the West Country speech with care and treats both the curate's gentleness and the villagers' rough justice with sympathy.
a-daughter-of-eve:
Honoré de Balzac builds his novel around two sisters, the Maries of his first chapter's title, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation. One sister has married for rank and lives in Parisian society; the other has married a banker and keeps a respectable home. A confidence between the sisters opens the tale, and a celebrated man enters it.

Chapters follow the actress Florine, a romantic love pursued through letters, rising debt, and a crisis named plainly in the contents: Suicide. The husband's triumph closes the book. Balzac studies how boredom, vanity, and fine feeling can wreck a good woman in a world that watches women closely and judges them harshly.
a-dozen-ways-of-love: Lily Dougall explores a dozen ways of love in short stories. Her chapters treat young love, a marriage made in heaven, thrift, a taint in the blood, and witchcraft. Other tales follow a commercial traveler, a syndicate baby, and a girl who believed in love. Dougall writes of love in its many forms with sympathy and wit.
a-fool-for-love: Francis Lynde tells of a fool for love aboard a limited train. The hero takes passage in a Missouri December, and an engine switched and an itinerary changed set the plot moving. Chapters follow a landslide, a rajah's order, and the majesty of the law. Lynde writes a railroad romance of adventure and devotion.
a-zola-dictionary-the-characters-of-the-:
J. G. Patterson's A Zola Dictionary, prepared at Edinburgh in May 1912, indexes the people of Émile Zola's Rougon-Macquart novels. A biographical and critical introduction opens the volume. Synopses of the plots follow, arranged in the reading order Zola himself indicated. A map and the family's genealogical tree complete the apparatus.

Twenty novels and hundreds of characters pass under Patterson's alphabetical hand. Each entry condenses a life from Zola's own words, so far as condensation allowed. He relied on the recognized biographies by Alexis, Sherrard, and Vizetelly, his prefatory note records. The dictionary serves readers lost in the vast clan of Rougons and Macquarts, legitimate and illegitimate branches alike. Heredity, Zola's ruling idea, becomes visible in the tree. Reference works date quickly, but this one preserves how Edwardian England organized its Zola.
adventures-of-a-sixpence-in-guernsey-by-: A Native of Guernsey follows a single sixpence as it passes from hand to hand around the island, letting each new owner tell a piece of local life. Through shopkeepers, sailors, and country folk, the coin's journey sketches Guernsey manners, trades, and talk in the mid-nineteenth century. The device gives the book both a light plot and a portrait of an island community.
affairs-of-state-being-an-account-of-cer: Burton Egbert Stevenson sends an American family into comic peril in the land of windmills, where court intrigue and romance upset their holiday plans. The story follows wiles, disguises, and narrow escapes as ordinary travellers are swept into affairs of state far above their station. Light, brisk, and good-humoured, it is an early example of the Ruritanian romance.
american-political-ideas-viewed-from-the: John Fiske delivers American political ideas viewed from universal history, in lectures given at the Royal Institution of Great Britain in May 1880. Dedicated in spirit to Tocqueville, the lectures place American democracy in a long story of political growth. Fiske argues with clarity and optimism for the federal idea as a stage in human progress.
angel-agnes-the-heroine-of-the-yellow-fe: Charles Wesley Alexander tells of Angel Agnes, the heroine of the yellow fever plague in Shreveport. The story honours a woman whose nursing and courage stood out when fever struck the city. Alexander's account preserves a local heroine's memory, in the sentimental style of its time. Her name lived on in local praise long after.
beneath-the-banner-being-narratives-of-n:
F. J. Cross gathered these narratives of noble lives and brave deeds in a second edition of 1895, under a motto from Gordon: I have done my best for the honour of our country. Upwards of sixty short lives were promised for young readers. Contents name Alice Ayres, the nurse girl; Sir Samuel Baker, the slave-trade warrior; Grace Darling; Father Damien, friend of lepers; and Sir John Franklin in the Arctic.

Each life is told as an anecdote of duty at the sharp end. One sea rescue has Smith swim out to the drowning Bangura, exhaust himself supporting the man, and vanish with him under the water while two more men plunge in. Case and Chew, two working-men heroes, stand beside Cochrane and Colin Campbell of the thin red line. The book is Victorian hero-worship in pocket form, meant for prize-giving and Sunday reading.
benefits-forgot-a-story-of-lincoln-and-m:
Honoré Willsie, later Morrow, published this short novel with Stokes in 1917, illustrated by Charles E. Cartwright. Her frontispiece gives the heart of it: Lincoln bids a young man come here, sit down, and write a letter to his mother. Four chapters carry the plot — the donation party, the circuit rider, war, and Mr. Lincoln. Jason, the hero, is a preacher's son on the Illinois frontier.

His father's circuit-riding depended, the family said, on the horse Pilgrim. The animal knew his master was forgetful and would not budge if the saddle-bags were left behind. When Pilgrim balked, father knew. Jason's quarrel with his mother, his father's death, and enlistment lead him at last before Lincoln himself, who reads the boy's ingratitude and prescribes the letter home. A Lincoln anecdote, expanded with love.
bibb-narrative:
Henry Bibb published his Narrative of his life and adventures in 1849. Born enslaved in Kentucky, Bibb escaped more than once, and each recapture cost him dearly. The book became a bestseller in the abolitionist movement.

Bibb tells how he left his wife and child to gain freedom, then risked return trips to free them. He describes slave markets, patrols, and the grief of families torn apart. His path later crossed the Cherokee country, where slavery also held Native people. Bibb went on to edit a Black newspaper in Canada for refugee readers. His account includes letters and notices meant to prove his tale true.
blind-love:
Blind Love is a novel by Wilkie Collins, left unfinished at his death and completed by Walter Besant. Collins builds the tale in three periods around Iris Henley, Lord Harry, and the friend who loves her, Hugh Mountjoy. A shady doctor, Vimpany, and his wife press in from the edges.

Cards, a registered packet, and a father's message set the early plot in motion. Marriage brings no peace: quarrels, a keyhole watch, and a hospital secret deepen the trap. Fanny, the faithful maid, tells much of the late story in her own voice. A dead man's likeness, a wife's return, and a last find bring the threads together. Besant's ending keeps Collins's plan, so readers get the whole design the author laid out.
brannon-s-picture-of-the-isle-of-wight-t:
George Brannon printed and published Brannon's Picture of the Isle of Wight at Wootton, where he had lived near forty years. Brannon, an artist, aims his guide at visitors who can spare only two or three days for the island tour. His index plan shows what to see, and how, at a glance.

Routes run from Cowes and Ryde to Ventnor, Bonchurch, and the Pulpit Rock. Views east over Sandown and west to Newport and Carisbrooke get careful staging in words. Seats and houses of note end the book in a long resident list. Brannon keeps talk short and points the eye instead. Hurried tourists of the steamboat age got a working guide from a local hand, not a London hack.
britannica-1911-ablative: Ablative is the headword of a short grammar entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry names a noun case whose first sense is direction from, from Latin ablatum, taken away. Latin, its chief home, stretches the case to instrument, agent, place, time, and manner, with or without a preposition. Sanskrit, Zend, Oscan, and Umbrian hold the case too. The ablative absolute, a noun and participle standing free of the sentence's frame, closes the notice.
britannica-1911-accusative:
Accusative, in grammar, is a case of the noun, the form a word takes when it stands as the object of a verb's action or shows the destination of motion. The 1911 Britannica entry is a compact definition with a history of the name inside it. Latin accusativus translates a Greek phrase meaning the case concerned with cause and effect, built on the Greek word for a cause.

That origin explains a puzzle for learners. The name seems to promise blame or charging, yet the case simply marks what an action acts on or where movement ends. Readers of Latin, Greek, and German grammar meet the term constantly, and the entry fixes its real job in one sentence.
britannica-1911-aimard-gustave:
Aimard, Gustave, the pen-name of the French novelist Olivier Gloux, is noticed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paris in September 1818, he lived a roving, adventurous youth and early manhood. Those travels stocked him with material for fiction. He turned it into numerous romances written in the manner of J. Fenimore Cooper, the American frontier novelist.

Among his best books the entry names Les Trappeurs de l'Arkansas, the trappers of Arkansas, from 1858. La Grande flibuste followed in 1860, then Nuits mexicaines in 1863 and La Foret vierge in 1870. The titles alone show his ground: trappers, freebooters, Mexico, and the virgin forest. Aimard died in Paris in June 1883. Many of his novels were translated into English, carrying his version of the American wilds back to English-speaking readers.
britannica-1911-alcove: Alcove, an architectural term defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, names a recess in a room. Such a recess is usually screened off from the main space by pillars, a balustrade, or drapery, giving the room a smaller side space set apart within it. The word reached English through the Spanish alcova, and behind that from the Arabic al-quobbah, where quobbah means a vault. Its path from an Arabic word for a vaulted place to a European word for a screened recess is the whole substance of the brief entry.
britannica-1911-autoclave:
Autoclave is a strong closed metal vessel. Liquids can be heated inside it above boiling point. Pressure makes that heating possible. The word indicates a self-closing vessel literally. Internal pressure maintains the joints' tightness in theory. Actual apparatus often lacks that characteristic, though. Papin's digester of 1681 was the prototype. That device is still used in cooking today.

Chemical industry employs autoclaves much more widely. Candle manufacture uses them in various forms. Coal-tar colour manufacture uses them too. An agitator often passes through a stuffing-box. Contents can thus be stirred during heating. Renewable linings protect against corrosive substances. Such substances would attack the metal otherwise. The entry is a compact industrial definition. It balances etymology against modern factory practice.
britannica-1911-brive:
Brive, or Brives-la-Gaillarde, is a town of south-central France, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Correze, 62 miles south-south-east of Limoges on the Orleans railway line from Paris to Montauban. The town held 14,954 people in 1906 and its commune 20,636. It lies on the left bank of the Correze in a wide, fertile plain where major roads and railways meet.

Old town walls have given place to shady boulevards, though many narrow winding streets and ancient houses remain inside them. Outside lie modern quarters and a fine promenade planted with plane trees running to the river. It holds the chief restaurants and the theatre, plus a statue of Marshal Brune, a native of Brive. A fine bridge crosses to suburbs on the right bank.
britannica-1911-bromsgrove:
Bromsgrove is a market town in Worcestershire, England, 12 miles north-north-east of Worcester, with its station a mile from town on the Midland railway's Bristol to Birmingham line. Its urban district held 8418 people in 1901. It sits in pleasant rolling country near the foot of the Lickey Hills, where the railway climbs for 2 miles up one of the steepest long gradients in England.

Half-timbered houses from 1572 onward survive in its streets, and St John's church, Perpendicular and earlier work, stands picturesquely on a rise with a tall tower and spire. A famed grammar school founded by Edward VI, with university scholarships, heads its schools. Cloth, once the staple trade, has given way to nails and buttons as the chief makes. The river Salwarpe drives many mills nearby and Midland railway carriage works stand by the town.
britannica-1911-captive:
A captive is a person captured in warfare. The word comes from the Latin capere, to take. This very short 1911 Britannica entry gives the term's place in law. In international law the word has been displaced. “Prisoner of war” is now the standard term instead. The treatment of such prisoners is set out fully elsewhere.

Chapter two of the Hague regulations covers the subject. Those rules were annexed to the Hague Convention of 1907. That convention treats the laws and customs of war on land. The entry points readers to the articles on the peace conference and on war. It also cites Sir Thomas Barclay's supplement on international practice. That work compares the texts of 1899 and 1907 side by side. The notice itself is only a few lines long. It defines the word and sends the reader onward.
britannica-1911-chive:
Chive is a plant article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a hardy herb that comes back year after year. Its Latin name is given in the text. The plant bears small, narrow bulbs in tufts on short root stocks. Its leaves are long, round, and hollow.

The article ranges the plant across the north temperate world. It grows wild in the north of England and in Cornwall. Rocky pastures across Europe and Asiatic Russia suit it, as do hill districts in the south of Europe. Growers raise it for its leaves. The leaves stand in for young onions in salads and soups. The text tells how to split the roots in spring or fall. It adds that the leaves should be cut often to keep them tender.
britannica-1911-citta-della-pieve:
Città della Pieve is a town and episcopal see of Umbria, Italy, in the province of Perugia, set 1,666 feet above the sea. It stands three miles north-east of its station on the railway between Chiusi and Orvieto. Its people numbered 8,381 in 1901, forming a small hill town in the province. Etruscan tombs have been found in the neighbourhood around the town.

Fame rests on one native son, the painter Pietro Vannucci, known as Perugino, who was born here. The town possesses several of his works for visitors to see. None of those works, the entry judges plainly, is of the first rank. It is also not certain that the present town stands on an ancient site, despite the Etruscan finds nearby. Birthplace honour, a bishop's seat and old tombs make the whole of this brief notice.
britannica-1911-conclave:
Conclave strictly means a room locked with a key, from Latin roots. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says that plain sense had faded in English by its time. The word now names the locked assembly of cardinals who elect a pope. Strict seclusion of those electors gives the system its name as well.

Early pope choices at Rome used a far more open method instead. Clergy, people, and nearby bishops all played a part in those days. Acclaim rather than counted votes often settled the outcome then. Cabals brought fights, bloodshed, and rival popes called antipopes at times. Civil power was later called in to curb such abuse.
britannica-1911-cove:
Cove is a word used most for a small inlet or sheltered bay in a coast-line. In English dialect it also names a cave or a hollow in a mountain-side. Its Old English form is cofa. Kin forms run through German, Norwegian and other Teutonic tongues. It has no link with alcove, cup, coop or cave, the entry is at pains to say.

Its first use was tighter than the coastal sense. It named a small chamber, cell or inner recess in a room or building. From that root grows its building sense. In architecture a cove is any concave moulding of a set kind. The term fits the curved sweep that rises from a tall room's cornice to the ceiling edge. In half-timbered work, coving names the curved soffit under a jutting window. In the 1700s it also named the curve that bore a house gutter.
britannica-1911-crauck-gustave:
Gustave Crauck (1827–1905) was a French sculptor born at Valenciennes. He died in that same town, where a museum for his works was built in his honour. The world at large knew little of him in his long life. All the same, he ranks among the best modern sculptors of France in the entry's judgment. Paris holds three of his public works in plain view.

His Coligny monument stands in the rue de Rivoli in that city. His Victory stands in the Place des Arts et Métiers. Among his finest works is his Combat of the Centaur. He laboured on that piece for thirty years in all. The figure of the Lapith in it was modelled on the athlete Eugene Sandow. In 1907 a show of his works was held at the École des Beaux-Arts. That show came two years after his death.
britannica-1911-curve:
Curve is a word from the Latin for bent, and this 1911 Britannica entry treats it as a topic in geometry, told through its history. In common speech a curve is a line that bends steadily out of the straight without making an angle. A proper definition, the entry says, needs the terms of geometry. The article works through the leading ideas in the order they were reached and grown.

First, a curve is a line, or a continuous system of points of a single endless run. Such a curve can be seen as a finished path, or as the track of a moving point. Either way it is the set of all points that meet a given condition. The circle is the plainest case: all points at a set distance from a fixed centre.
britannica-1911-dative:
Dative is a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a word used in grammar and in law. The name comes from a Latin word for giving. In grammar the dative is the case of the indirect object. It marks the person or thing to whom or for whom a thing is given or done.

In law the word marks a thing that can be given or taken at will, as set against a thing held for good. In Scots law it names persons or powers named by a court, such as an executor named by the court and not by a will. Roman law used it for a guardian named in a will. The hosted page opens with the tail of the Datia article before this entry starts.
britannica-1911-endive:
Endive is a yearly plant grown for the table, of the same great family as the daisy. The 1911 Britannica article says it is thought to have come to Europe from the East Indies. Some hold that it is native to Egypt instead. It has been grown in England for more than three hundred years. John Gerarde named it in his Herbal of 1597. Its kinds fall in two groups. The curled, narrow-leaved kind serves most for salads. The broad-leaved Batavian kind is grown for the cook pot.

The plant needs a light, rich, dry soil in an open, sunny place. For the main crop in England, seed is sown in the last weeks of June. Seed goes in drills four inches apart and is lightly covered. When the shoots reach an inch they are thinned out. At a month old they are set out a foot or more apart.
britannica-1911-feuillet-octave:
Octave Feuillet is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a French novelist and dramatist. He lived from 1821 to 1890. He was born at Saint-Lo in the department of Manche. His father was a Norman gentleman of learning and standing. Nervous excitability marked the father all his life. Octave inherited that trait, though in lesser degree. His mother died in his infancy at home.

The boy was sent to a famed school in Paris. He was meant for the diplomatic service after school. In 1840 he told his father he would write for a living. A stormy scene followed that bold announcement. His father cut him off for the choice he made. He went back to Paris and lived by scant journalism. With Paul Bocage he began to write for the stage. That stage work kept him alive for three years.
britannica-1911-flaubert-gustave:
Gustave Flaubert (1821-1880), French novelist, was born at Rouen on 12 December 1821. His father was a surgeon at Rouen. Many of his traits live again in Charles Bovary, Flaubert's own creation. His mother came from old Norman families. Educated at Rouen, he went to Paris in 1840 to study law, though he had been busy with literature since he was eleven. Paris displeased him, and he travelled in the Pyrenees and Corsica.

After his father and sister died in 1846, Flaubert left Paris and the law to make a home for his mother at Croisset, near Rouen. That house by the Seine stayed his home for the rest of his life. The long entry follows him into the writer he became. It treats his life, his work habits and his novels, with Madame Bovary at their head.
britannica-1911-foster-sir-clement-le-ne:
Sir Clement Le Neve Foster (1841-1904), English geologist and mineralogist, was the second son of Peter Le Neve Foster, long secretary of the Society of Arts. He was born at Camberwell on 23 March 1841. Educated at Boulogne and Amiens, he studied at the Royal School of Mines in London and at the mining college of Freiburg in Saxony. In 1860 he joined the Geological Survey in England, working first in the Wealden area and then in Derbyshire.

With William Topley, Foster sent the Geological Society a classic paper of 1865 on the superficial deposits of the Medway valley. It argued ably that rain and rivers had sculptured the Weald. He left the Survey that same year and gave his attention to mining. His name stands with the study of mines and minerals in Victorian Britain.
britannica-1911-foxglove:
Foxglove is a genus of biennial and perennial plants of the family Scrophulariaceae. The common or purple foxglove, Digitalis purpurea, grows in dry hilly pastures, rocky places and roadsides across much of Europe. In Great Britain it ranges from Cornwall and Kent to Orkney, though it is missing from Shetland and some eastern counties. It loves siliceous soils and is not found in the Jura or the Swiss Alps, a distribution the entry maps with care for the field botanist.

The plant's marks are given in full. Its stem is erect, roundish and downy, leafy below, and from eighteen inches to five feet or more in height. The leaves are alternate, notched, wrinkled and dull green, paler and downy beneath. The root is a bundle of slender whitish fibres. Its hanging flowers stand on one side of the stem. The article goes on to the plant's kinds and uses.
britannica-1911-kahn-gustave:
Gustave Kahn (1859– ) was a French poet, born at Metz on the 21st of December 1859. His segment sits in a hosted file shared with the Kagera, Kahlur, and Kahnis entries. He was schooled in Paris and began to write for small Paris reviews. After four years in Africa he came back to Paris in 1885.

In 1886 he founded a weekly review, La Vogue, where many of his early poems appeared. That autumn he joined Jean Moréas and Paul Adam in a short lived journal, Le Symboliste, which preached the poetic doctrine of Mallarmé. In 1888 he became an editor of the Revue indépendante. He claimed to be the first writer of free verse, and set out his method in a preface to his Premiers poèmes of 1897. Later work includes a sound history of the movement, Symbolistes et décadents, in 1902.
britannica-1911-mosquito-coast-and-reser:
Mosquito Coast and Reserve, a strip of land in Nicaragua on the Caribbean Sea, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Officially it was styled the department of Zelaya. About fifteen thousand people lived there at the count in the entry. The strip runs about two hundred miles from north to south. It reaches inland for about forty miles on average.

Bluefields, the capital and largest town, had about two thousand people. It had a good harbour, a Moravian mission, and steam ship links to New Orleans. Fruit, most of all bananas, was shipped out. The coast takes its name from the Miskito people, whose name settlers warped into Mosquito. The entry traces English claims there from a first settlement in 1630. Britain held a protectorate claim for near two hundred years, in the face of rival claims.
britannica-1911-muscle-and-nerve:
Muscle and Nerve is the subject of a body science article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The article starts with a key trait of living matter in muscle cells. Those cells free stored energy in a way that does work. The work comes from movement, as parts of the cell change their pull and the cell grows short. That shortening is called contraction.

The text explains that a cell keeps its bulk while it changes shape. One width grows as the other shrinks. It then sorts kinds of contraction. A steady, even pull in the walls of hollow organs and the heart comes from the tissue's own life. In limb muscles, steady pull is kept up by nerve signals in a reflex loop. Sense organs in muscle help start that loop. Readers get a clear base for how muscle and nerve act together.
britannica-1911-ogive: Ogive names the diagonal ribs of a vault in building work. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that the French origin of the word is not clear. In France the term is more often used for the pointed arch itself. From that use it became a name for Gothic building as a whole, often called le style ogival.
britannica-1911-peacock-thomas-love:
Thomas Love Peacock (1785–1866) was an English novelist and poet born at Weymouth on the 18th of October 1785. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows him from a private school and a brief taste of business to a life of letters on family means. His first books were poems of small merit, and his plays were never acted.

In 1812 he met Shelley, whose near daily company he enjoyed at Great Marlow in 1817. His turn to novels began with Headlong Hall in 1816, and Nightmare Abbey and his best long poem, Rhododaphne, followed. Maid Marian came in 1822, The Misfortunes of Elphin in 1829, and Crotchet Castle in 1831. From 1819 he worked at India House, rising to chief examiner in 1836. There he made steam navigation to India his own cause and oversaw iron steamers in 1839 and 1840.
britannica-1911-perspective:
Perspective is the subject of an entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin term meaning to see through. In maths it names the art of drawing solid objects on a flat surface. A good drawing strikes the eye as the object itself does.

The entry builds the idea from projection, treated in a linked article. If all points in a figure are cast from a fixed centre onto a plane, each point has a match. A full picture from one projection works only when each ray holds one point to be cast. The text works through when that holds and what follows for drawing.
britannica-1911-pirmez-octave:
Octave Pirmez lived from 1832 to 1883 and was a Belgian author of quiet, sad books. The short Britannica life of 1911 places his birth at Chatelineau. He came of a well known Belgian house with men of letters in it. His own life was calm and spent at his castle of Acoz in Hainaut.

Pirmez loved the French romantic school and let it shape his prose. His books trace his inner life year by year in frank terms. They include Les Feuillees in 1862 and Jours de solitude in 1869. Heures de philosophie came in 1881, near the end of his life. A deep gloom runs through all his work, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-tamatave:
Tamatave, called Toamasina by its own people, is the chief seaport of Madagascar, and the 1911 Britannica gives it a port entry. It stands near the middle of the east coast of the island. A coral reef forms a broad, fair harbour with two mouths, and the town is built on a sandy spit. Good shops line its main streets, and foreign consuls sit there.

The port serves the capital and the inland trade of the island. Imports ran to cloth, flour foods, and iron and steel goods. Exports ran to gold dust, raffia, hides, rubber, and live beasts. Steamers linked it with Europe, Mauritius, and Ceylon, and 46 per cent of the island's foreign trade passed through it. Plague struck in 1898 and 1900, but the draining of near marshes brought gains. A telegraph line of 180 miles tied the port to the capital.
britannica-1911-ticket-of-leave:
Ticket of Leave is a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains a pass in the English prison system of the time. A convict who had served a set part of a term in good order earned the pass. With it he could live free in a half free state and earn his own bread.

The entry lists the strict terms printed on the pass. The man must report to the police soon after release and then each month. He must work in an honest trade and sleep at the address he gave. Any move must be told to the police at both ends of the move. A breach of the terms could send him back to serve the rest.
britannica-1911-trave:
Trave, a river of north Germany, gets a short course entry in the 1911 Britannica. It rises in the Lübeck principality of Oldenburg, between Eutin and Ahrensbock. At first it flows south through small lakes and marshes. Then it turns west through flat, sandy banks into Schleswig-Holstein. At Oldesloe it bends south and becomes fit for boats.

From there it runs east, takes in the Stecknitz, and passes the city of Lübeck. The Stecknitz canal, built by Lübeck merchants in 1398, links it with the Elbe. The river then flows into the Baltic at Travemünde, after a course of 58 miles. Its lower reach from Lübeck to the sea has been dredged to 25 feet deep. That depth lets sea going ships lie at the wharves of Lübeck itself. The entry is brief but complete: source, turns, canal link, and sea outlet are all fixed.
britannica-1911-treasure-trove:
Treasure Trove is a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about hidden wealth found in the ground. The term covers coin, bullion, and gold or silver goods found buried, with no owner to be found. What is found in the sea or on the surface does not count.

The article traces the right to such finds through past law. In Roman law half went to the finder and half to the owner of the land. As feudal rule spread, the prince claimed the right as lord of all land. In England the right has long rested with the Crown. A finder must report the find to the coroner at once. An inquest then rules on what the find is. To hide a find is a crime in England, though not in Scotland.
britannica-1911-zouave:
Zouave was the name given to some foot regiments in the French army, as set out in this 1911 Britannica article. The corps was first raised in Algeria in 1831, at first with men drawn from the Zouaves, a Berber tribe of the Jurjura hills. A third battalion was added in 1838, under Lamoricière.

Later the native corps changed, and the Zouave battalions became a purely French body. Three regiments were formed in 1852, and a fourth, of the Imperial Guard, in 1854. Their first service outside Algeria came in the Crimean War. The article also notes the Papal Zouaves, raised in 1860 to defend the Papal states and disbanded after the war of 1870.
brown-narrative:
William Wells Brown escaped slavery in Missouri in 1834 and published his Narrative in 1847. Brown had worked as a steamboat hand on the Mississippi, which gave him his chance to run. The book went through several editions in a few years.

He tells of his hire to a slave trader, the coffles on the road, and the suffering he witnessed. After escape he became an abolitionist lecturer in America and Britain. Brown later wrote Clotel, often called the first novel by an African American. His Narrative shows the keen storyteller he already was on the lecture stage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Sainte-Geneviève describes the Paris abbey founded by King Clovis as a college of clerics, later canons regular. By 1147 secular canons officiated there, but Louis the Seventh and the pope, witnessing disorders, resolved to restore regular discipline.

At Suger and St. Bernard's request, Gildwin, first Abbot of Saint-Victor, sent Odo, his prior, to lead the reform. Difficulties followed, but order prevailed and some canons joined, including the young Canon William, famed for virtue and learning. At Bishop Absalon of Roskild's request William went to Denmark to reform a monastery on the Isle of Eskil, enduring trials, obstacles and persecutions in the work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baltasar-de-e:
Baltasar de Echave, called the Elder, was a painter born at Zumaya in Spain late in the sixteenth century. He died in Mexico about the middle of the seventeenth century. He ranked among the earliest Spanish artists to reach Mexico, arriving with Sebastian Arteaga and Alonzo Vasquez. Tradition says his wife, also a painter, taught him.

His subjects were chiefly religious, and his skill in composition, charm of color, and tenderness recall Guercino. The National Academy of San Carlos in Mexico City holds many of his best pictures, from the Adoration of the Magi to Saint Cecilia. More hang in the Profesa church, and fifteen altar panels stand in Santiago Tlaltelolco. His cathedral Candelaria and a San Sebastian are also noted, the latter believed to be his wife's work. He also wrote on the Biscayan language.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-kervyn-:
Baron Kervyn de Lettenhove was a Belgian statesman and writer of history, born near Bruges in 1817, who died there in 1891. Sent to the Chamber of Representatives in 1861, he debated foreign affairs and public schools keenly. In 1870 his party took power, and he received the Interior post. A mistaken Limburg governor pick forced him to quit, and he slowly left politics for history work.

Already in 1856 the French Academy had crowned his Studies on Froissart's Chronicles. Touring Europe's book rooms and archives, he gathered data that revised common views on several points. His grave, polished, somewhat puffed-up style drew charges of bias to Elizabeth, William the Silent, and Marnix, without sufficient reason. His major works span Flanders's history, Commines's letters, Burgundian Belgium, Mary Stuart, and ties with England under Philip II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-categorical-i:
The categorical imperative is Immanuel Kant's term for the moral law as reason itself lays it down. Kant starts from the good will. Only a will that acts from duty, out of respect for the law and not from inclination or hoped-for results, counts as good without qualification. The law commands respect because it is universal and necessary, binding every rational being alike.

Kant states the rule as acting only on a maxim that could hold as a universal law for all rational beings. The article then weighs this account against Kant's own theoretical philosophy, noting a tension between the two that makes moral necessity look close to fatalism. Kant set out the imperative in 1785 and again in his Critique of Practical Reason in 1788.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-citta-della-p:
Citta della Pieve, a city of obscure origin in Umbria's Perugia province, was certainly an episcopal see by the eleventh century. In 1099 its bishop was expelled by the Ghibellines. Paschal the Second later joined it to the Diocese of Chiusi. Clement the Eighth re-established it as a separate see in 1601, with Fabrizio Paolucci of the Counts of Cabulo as first bishop.

In 1642, while Giovanni Battista Carcarasio was bishop, German soldiers of the Duke of Parma sacked the city. The diocese answers directly to the Holy See. Its cathedral, dedicated to Saints Gervasius and Protasius, was reportedly built at Saint Ambrose's urging. The diocese counts sixty thousand people, thirty-three parishes, eighty-six churches and chapels, sixty-five secular priests, and four houses of women religious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conclave:
Austin Dowling's entry explains the conclave, from Latin cum, with, and clavis, key: a place securely closed. It means both the closed hall prepared for cardinals electing a pope and the assembly itself. In present form it dates from the end of the thirteenth century. Earlier ways of filling Peter's See belong to the Papal Elections entry. Dowling treats the method's history and the ceremonial itself.

History opens at Viterbo in 1271, where an election dragged over two years and nine months until local authorities shut the cardinals in. Stringent rules drew opposition, yet early conclave elections proved the principle sound. Ceremonial runs from the camerlengo's verification of the pope's death to the walling off of Vatican apartments, cells for cardinals and conclavists, perhaps two hundred and fifty persons inside. Four forms of election stand: scrutinium, compromissum, accessus, and quasi-inspiratio, with secret ballot and a two-thirds vote.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dove:
The dove appears in Christian antiquity both as a symbol and as a vessel for the Eucharist. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry finds it most often as a sign of the Holy Spirit, above all in scenes of the baptism of Christ and of Pentecost. Saint Gregory the Great is shown with a dove on his shoulder, marking inspiration and divine guidance. After Clovis's baptism, a dove of gold was hung in the baptistery at Reims.

Dove-shaped vessels were also hung over baptismal fonts, and the dove marked martyrdom, showing the Spirit granting fortitude. Gifts of silver towers with golden doves from Constantine and later popes fill the old papal book of lives. The entry thus follows one gentle bird through art, liturgy, and the treasures of Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eve:
Eve is the first woman of the Bible, wife of Adam and mother of Cain, Abel, and Seth. Her Hebrew name, Hawwah, appears only five times in Scripture, and Genesis links it with the verb to live, since she was mother of all the living. The Bible's account of her lies almost wholly in Genesis chapters two, three, and four. The first story tells simply that mankind was made male and female, while the second tells how God formed woman from man's rib.

In the story of the Fall, the serpent tempts Eve, she tempts Adam, and shame and remorse follow their eating. For her share she is sentenced to sorrow in childbirth and to life under her husband's power. Yet God also promises enmity between her seed and the serpent, until her seed, the future Redeemer, crushes its head.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-expectative:
Expectative means the advance grant of a church benefice that is not yet vacant. It falls vacant in due course, regularly on the death of its present holder. The Third Lateran Council in 1179 forbade such promises, renewing an older ban, and Boniface VIII widened the ban. Yet through the Middle Ages chapters still gave expectatives for canon stalls, and the Holy See let chapters name four canons that way.

Popes from the twelfth century granted them straight, and charged another churchman with investing the appointee later. Delegates of the Holy See, universities, and certain princes also won the privilege, with limits. The practice bred grave abuses, above all during the Western Schism. Trent swept expectatives away, save a coadjutor named with right of succession for bishops and abbots, plus prefects Apostolic. Trent allows the only expectatives still in use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-jean-ba:
Felix Neve was a Belgian Orientalist and philologist of the University of Louvain. Born at Ath in 1816, he took his doctorate at Louvain in 1838. He studied under Lassen, Tiersch, and Burnouf at Bonn, Munich, and Paris. In 1841 he took the university chair of Greek and Latin literature.

Neve taught Sanskrit at Louvain for thirty-six years with unsparing energy and success. He translated chosen Rig-Veda hymns and the Indian drama of Rama's story. He also worked on Armenian texts, prayers, hymns, and histories. Retired in 1877, he published steadily for fifteen more years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-perreyv:
Paris priest Henri Perreyve, born in 1831 to a law professor, gave up law for philosophy and theology and helped restore the Oratory in France. With the Perraud brothers and Father Gratry under Father Pététol, he rebuilt the congregation and was ordained in 1858. He served as chaplain at Lycée Saint-Louis and took the Sorbonne chair of church history in 1861 until illness stopped his lectures.

Friend to Ozanam, Montalembert, Cochin, and Lacordaire, he won young men above all by a kind and affectionate nature. His works include a critique of the Gospels of 1859, talks on the Catholic Church, a sick person's day, biographies and panegyrics, and first communion memories. Sermons and meditations on John and on holy orders complete the list. Letters were published after his early death in 1865.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-cosgrov:
Henry Cosgrove, second Bishop of Davenport, Iowa, was born at Williamsport, Pennsylvania, in 1834 and emigrated to Iowa with his parents in 1845. Ordained priest in 1857, he took charge of St. Marguerite's Church, Davenport, in 1861, and after Bishop McMullen's death administered the diocese before his own consecration on 20 July 1884. He was the first native-born American named to a see west of the Mississippi.

Short as this entry is, it marks a turning point in the American hierarchy: leadership passing from missionary bishops sent from abroad to men raised on the frontier they would govern. Cosgrove died at Davenport on 23 December 1906, having spent nearly half a century in the service of the Iowa church he had joined as an eleven-year-old immigrant child.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-capgrave:
John Capgrave was an Augustinian friar, historian, and theologian of fifteenth-century Norfolk. Born at Lynn in 1393, he was ordained about 1417 and professed an Augustinian at Lynn. He became doctor of divinity and later provincial of his order, and died at Lynn in 1464.

His name is best known for the Nova Legenda Angliae, the first full collection of English saints' lives. It was really compiled by John of Tynemouth and only edited and rearranged by Capgrave. Apart from that, his own works prove unusual scholarship: lives of Henry VI's worthies, of Humphrey Duke of Gloucester, and of St. Gilbert and St. Katharine, a Chronicle of England to 1417, commentaries on many Bible books, a work on the creeds, and sermons and lectures, many still in manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josse-clichto:
Josse Clichtove was a Flemish theologian of the Sorbonne who fought Luther with pen and council. Born at Nieuport in 1472, he studied at Louvain and Paris, took his theology doctorate in 1506, and became a Sorbonne professor. In 1515 he took charge of the studies of Louis Guillard, bishop-elect of Tournai, and followed him to Tournai and Chartres.

Clichtove began with commentaries on Aristotle and the Fathers and early championed reform of studies. Later he gave himself almost wholly to opposing Luther, gathering the Council of Sens' arguments into a volume and writing Antilutherus and a defense of the Church against Lutheran claims. His works span nearly every branch of theology and philosophy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-love:
Love, in theology called charity, is the third and greatest of the divine virtues named by Paul. It is a gift poured into the heart that moves the will to cherish God above all things, and people for God's sake. It differs from natural liking, since it comes by divine infusion with sanctifying grace.

Its seat lies in the rational will, not in feeling alone. Its act is benevolent friendship: wishing God all honour and seeking it for him, as friends seek good for friends. Its motive is God's own goodness, loved for itself, not for reward, and its range covers God and neighbour alike. Later sections weigh hope, self-love, and the order of loving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nave:
A nave, architecturally, is the central, open space of a church, west of the choir or chancel, separated from it by a low wall or screen. Columns, shafts or piers divide it from the side aisles. It is roofed with timber or vaulted in masonry, and usually rises above the aisle roofs for high windows. Colloquially the term covers the worshippers' portion, including central and side aisles and crossing transepts.

The name comes from Latin navis, a ship, perhaps recalling Saint Peter's ship or Noah's Ark. The norm for all later developments, early Christian, Byzantine, Norman, medieval, Renaissance, lies in the Roman basilica, with its wide central area and aisles and galleries divided by columns and arches. In the third and fourth centuries the apse was pushed back behind a transverse nave or transept, and later nave, transept and apse met under a dome or tower at the crossing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neve:
Neve was a titular see of Arabia, suffragan of Bostra. Two of its bishops are known: Petronius, who attended Ephesus in 431, and Jobius, present at Chalcedon in 451. Isaac, a third bishop named by Le Quien about 540, was not Neve's bishop but Nineve's, living at the end of the seventh century.

The Diocese of Neve appears in Antioch's sixth-century Notitia, and George of Cyprus mentions the city in the next century. The Revue biblique published Greek inscriptions from the locality. A large Muslim village called Nawa, in the Hauran, now occupies the former see's site, and the ancient Christian church's tower still stands visible. Neve must not be confused with Mount Nebo, about 94 miles south of the town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-octave:
An octave, in liturgy, stretches a feast across eight days, though seven, not eight, rules Jewish festal reckoning. Each seventh day is a Sabbath, and the seventh month and year are sacred, and feasts like Azymes and Tabernacles last seven days, with Pentecost seven weeks after Passover.

Yet the eighth day kept its own role: circumcision fell on it, Tabernacles gained an eighth-day solemnity, and Temple dedications closed on it. The church took up that pattern, and the entry follows octaves from Jewish roots through Roman practice to their modern ranks and rules.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parasceve:
Parasceve, from the Greek for preparation, displaced the older prosabbaton and became the Hellenistic Jews' name for Friday. Greek church writers took it up after the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles. Jews first applied it to Friday afternoon, then to the whole day, since preparations for the Sabbath had to be made, as the King James Bible's Day of Preparation shows.

Law's minute observance demanded three meals of choicest food ready before sunset, and barred Friday afternoon business that might spill into the Sabbath. Augustus freed Jews from certain legal duties from the ninth hour. Parasceve also marked eves of sabbatic feasts, above all Nisan 15, first day of unleavened bread, whose eve in Judea stopped work at noon and in Galilee freed the whole day. Later pages trace its liturgical uses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-de-chome:
Paul de Chomedey de Maisonneuve was the founder of Montreal, born in Champagne early in the seventeenth century and dead at Paris on 9 September 1676. He served in the Dutch war at thirteen. Reading Jesuit Relations drew him to Canada. Jerome Lalemant proposed him to lead Royer de la Dauversiere's company to found Ville-Marie on Montreal island. Lauzon, the ex-governor, had ceded it for ten pounds of fish a year. Jeanne Mance, future foundress of the Hotel-Dieu, joined the party.

Governor Montmagny tried to stop the venture, holding the colonists at Sillery through winter 1641 to 1642. Maisonneuve landed on the island with his followers on 17 May 1642. Vimont said the first Mass, and the Blessed Sacrament stayed exposed all day, lit by fireflies in a phial. The colony, dedicated to the Virgin as Ville-Marie, stood at a waterways' crossing, ever alert against Iroquois attack.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-van-hov:
Peter van Hove was a Flemish Franciscan exegete, born at Rethy in the Campine and dying at Antwerp in 1793. Pupil of William Smits, founder of Antwerp's Musaeum Philologico-Sacrum, he trained Franciscan students in biblical languages, history, geography, and chronology for a critical, literal reading of Scripture. On Smits's death in 1770 he took over the flourishing school, which the French Revolution soon destroyed.

Before that post he published historical and archaeological theses. A 1765 portrait of first-century church life drew largely from Paul. Later works covered sacred images, the theocratic kingdom of Israel, and Christ as our Passover, the last giving an excellent Gospel chronology. His heavier labour was finishing Smits's Flemish Vulgate translation and commentary, sixteen folio volumes already edited when the task fell to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-genevieve:
Genevieve, patroness of Paris, saved her city twice: once by prayer against Attila, once by charity under siege. Born at Nanterre about 419 or 422 to Severus and Gerontia, likely respectable townspeople rather than poor peasants, she caught Germain of Auxerre's eye as a thoughtful child in 429. He foretold a life of sanctity drawing many virgins to God. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Paris to 512.

When Attila swept Gaul in 451, Parisians prepared to flee, but Genevieve urged penance and trust, promising the town would be spared. Attila turned toward Orléans, leaving Paris untouched. Years later, under Merowig's siege, her charity won clemency from Merowig, Childeric, and Clovis. She planned the church of Peter and Paul, begun by Clovis, where she was buried and miracles multiplied at her tomb.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-state-or-way-:
The state or way of the soul, purgative, illuminative, and unitive, maps Christian growth in grace. Theologians use state for a calling in life, as when Paul bids each man abide in the calling wherein he was called. States of perfection divide into clerical, religious, and secular, and religious states into contemplative, active, and mixed orders.

In a second sense state means stages of advancement in the supernatural life: the practice of all virtues, theological and moral, in outward and inward acts. Two elements combine: human effort and God's assisting grace, never wanting for acts God commands or inspires. Perfection advances with the energy and fidelity of souls answering grace. The purgative way cleanses sin, the illuminative enlightens the mind, and the unitive joins the soul to God in love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-carve:
Thomas Carve, whose true name was Carew, was an Irish historian born in County Tipperary in 1590 and probably dead by 1672. Ordained priest, he left Ireland as chaplain to an Irish regiment serving in Austria under Walter Butler, and later under Devereux. He marched through several campaigns of the Thirty Years' War, watching at first hand the events he would record.

His chief work, the Itinerarium, published at Mainz, Speyer and later London, gives a soldier-chaplain's account of that war. In 1640 he became chaplain to the English, Scottish and Irish forces in Austria, and from 1643 he lived at Vienna as a choral vicar of St. Stephen's Cathedral. His last book appeared at Sulzbach in 1672.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-occlev:
Thomas Occleve, also called Hoccleve, was an English poet born about 1368 who died in 1450. Almost all we know of him comes from his own poems. At about nineteen he took a clerkship in the Privy Seal Office, a post he held for at least twenty-four years. He drew a pension of ten pounds a year from 1399 and twenty pounds from 1424.

His La Male Regle of 1406 confesses a life of pleasure and dissipation, while his marriage in 1411 and his De Regimine Principum soon after show a reformed man. Linked always with Lydgate as a follower of Chaucer, he left three passages about Chaucer. He also left a portrait of him in the De Regimine manuscript, painted, he says, to keep the master's face in memory.
celsus-de-medicina-grieve:
James Grieve translated Celsus's De Medicina into English in 1756. Aulus Cornelius Celsus compiled the great Roman medical encyclopedia around 25 CE. Surgery, drugs, and diet all stand within his clear Latin survey.

Celsus gives the famous four signs of inflammation still taught today. Redness, swelling, heat, and pain define the condition in his words. He describes cataract surgery, bladder stones, and wound care in detail. Grieve's translation made the most readable ancient medical text English. Celsus was likely a gentleman compiler rather than a practicing doctor. His clarity preserved Greek medicine for Rome and for every century since.
christmas-eve:
Robert Browning's Christmas Eve is a long poem that begins on a stormy night outside a little country chapel. The speaker, kept waiting in the rain, squeezes into a crowded dissenting service and watches a congregation very different from himself.

From that chapel the poem moves outward, setting one way of worship against others and testing where true faith is found. Browning lets the speaker argue, doubt and imagine, so that the poem becomes a dramatic debate about belief rather than a simple nativity piece. Readers who know Browning's monologues will recognise the restless, questioning voice, and newcomers will find a vivid entry into Victorian religious argument.
crockett-narrative:
Davy Crockett published his Narrative of his own life in 1834, while serving in Congress from Tennessee. Crockett was already a folk hero of the frontier, and tall tales clung to his name. He wrote, he said, to tell the true story himself.

He recounts bear hunts, militia service under Andrew Jackson, and rough backwoods politics in his own spelling and slang. Humor runs through it all, even his feuds with President Jackson. Two years later Crockett died at the Alamo. The Narrative fixed his image as the coonskin-capped frontiersman, half real man and half legend of his own making.
cynthia-s-revels-or-the-fountain-of-self:
Ben Jonson wrote Cynthia's Revels as a court comedy in which Queen Cynthia judges courtiers drunk on self-love. Jonson, the sharpest wit of Shakespeare's London stage, aimed the satire at the Elizabethan court itself. Cynthia, a goddess figure standing for the queen, holds a revel that turns into a trial. A fountain has infected the courtiers with vanity.

Crites, a scholar with the author's own voice, watches fools parade their ruling follies. Amorphus, a traveler shapeless from copying every foreign fashion, tutors Asotus in nonsense. Anaides and other gallants boast, dance, and sing while their emptiness shows through the polish. Cynthia at last unmasks the company, fines the worst offenders, and orders a cleaner court. Songs and masque-like dances sweeten the attack for its audience. Readers find Jonson mixing flattery and rebuke in one glass: praise for the queen, scorn for the parasites around her throne.
december-love:
Robert Hichens's December Love is a novel of London society. It opens with Alick Craven, a Foreign Office man who has lived in the capital for years, apart from a spell of military service. Craven keeps interesting friends but holds himself apart from social bustle, a laziness that puzzles his acquaintance Francis Braybrooke.

Braybrooke knows everybody and delights in people above ideas. He takes pleasure in drawing new faces into his circle, and his talk sets the novel's social machinery in motion. Hichens watches how talk, introductions and reputations steer lives in drawing rooms and clubs, with Craven's reserve as the still centre. Readers who enjoy novels of manners, where character is revealed in conversation rather than action, will find December Love finely observed.
desert-love:
A romance of Egypt fills Joan Conquest's Desert Love, issued by the Macaulay Company of New York under copyright of 1920. Conquest had written Leonie of the Jungle. Three parts divide the tale, named the Seed, the Flower, and the Fruit.

Jill, a golden-haired, blue-eyed English girl, looks out on the East in the first chapter. Women in black robes and face veils sit at her feet, with gold crescents on their brows. Men in turbans and head cloths crowd round, and Bedouins stand apart in white. A sheik with beads slipping through his fingers watches the girl in the silence before dawn. Conquest writes the desert romance then in vogue, all heat, veils, and stern sheiks.
direct-legislation-by-the-citizenship-th:
Law made by the people themselves is the theme of J. W. Sullivan's book, issued by the True Nationalist Publishing Company of New York in 1893, under copyright of 1892. Its title names the tools: the initiative and the referendum. Contents promise Switzerland first, then the United States.

Three chapters study the Swiss at home: their direct law making, their public stewardship, and their common wealth. Towns there, Sullivan says, show general prosperity, with roads, bridges, and public buildings that speak of industry and freedom to use it. Emigration runs low, and many who leave are educated folk of means. A last part takes up direct law in the United States, and a close names it the way open to peaceful revolution. The book is a primer of a new reform.
doe-osti-2584738-self-driving-lab-to-aut:
Alex Baker and Shelby Conn describe a self-driving laboratory in Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2007404, dated June 2025. The Autonomous Alloy Prediction and Experimentation platform, called APEX, uses robotics and machine learning to design, build, and test alloy samples without human intervention. Livermore is building it with Cornell University under a Laboratory Directed Research and Development project.

APEX can 3D print, grind, polish, and characterize samples, processing upwards of 48 samples a day. Tests include microscope examination of the surface, diamond indentation to measure hardness, and crushing to assess compression response. Pure metals often lack the strength, hardness, or corrosion resistance a job needs. The platform aims to cut new alloy development from years of trial and error to months.
doe-osti-2584750-in-situ-real-time-diagn: Filed as LLNL-TR-2009427 in August 2025, this single conference poster comes from Dylan Levine, Viktor Sukhotskiy, Nicholas Watkins, and Eric Elton. It presents a live diagnostic for liquid metal jetting. That method prints metal parts from jets of molten drops. Levine rebuilt his past imaging setup for finer detail and faster capture. He then ran fast Fourier transforms on the mass-flow signal. The results expose system resonances. They also show drop shape shifts tied to melt height. Both findings help tune the printer for steady, even drops.
doe-osti-2588502-dispatch-manager-for-ne:
Tianchen Hu and Mark Messner of Argonne National Laboratory wrote this report, ANL-25/22, on new plumbing inside the NEML2 constitutive modeling library. NEML2 supplies the material behavior laws that the MOOSE simulation framework calls millions of times per run. Evaluating those laws one device at a time wastes modern hardware, which mixes CPUs and GPUs.

The answer is a dispatch manager. A modular set of dispatcher and scheduler classes packages batches of material point evaluations, moves them to the right device, manages device-specific memory, and synchronizes the results. It runs synchronously or asynchronously, handles device-aware tensor operations, and cuts memory transfer waste. Modularity is deliberate, so future computing backends can plug in. Benchmarks in the report show the system scaling on modern GPU architectures, with throughput well above the older single-device path. Multiscale simulations, which live or die on batch evaluation speed, are the intended winners.
doe-osti-2999827-abstract-for-crada-amon: Congjun Wang, Yahya Al-Majali and Frank Kraft set out this one-page abstract for a cooperative research agreement, AGMT-1579, among the National Energy Technology Laboratory, Ohio University and MetalKraft Technologies. Most transmission lines are ageing, with about 70 percent near the end of their working life, and plain metal conductors waste energy. The project will build carbon-metal composites, mixing graphite or graphene into aluminium, copper and other metals. The aim is conductors that carry current better and stand up longer than today's lines.
doe-osti-3015564-application-of-sammy-fo:
Checking irradiated samples without cutting them open is the aim of ORNL/TM-2025/4082, dated December 2025, which applies the SAMMY code to neutron transmission data from the VENUS beamline. Resonance patterns in transmitted neutrons reveal which isotopes sit inside a sealed sample and in what amounts. Luiz Leal led the author team.

The team folded VENUS's resolution function into SAMMY's analysis and built a search procedure for identifying sample contents. A hafnium isotope case study compares the standard SAMMY procedure against a modified implementation, showing where the standard fit succeeds and where the modification matters. Experimental transmission data are then analyzed end to end. The payoff is a non-destructive assay route for irradiated materials that cannot be dissolved or sectioned for ordinary chemistry.
doe-osti-3021677-development-of-next-gen:
LLNL CRADA final report TC02412, by Sichi Li and Simon Pang with Benjamin Greydanus, tells of joint work with Global Thermostat on keeping direct air capture sorbents alive longer. Amine-based sorbents grab carbon dioxide from air but slowly oxidize, losing capacity. The main one studied is polyethylenimine (PEI). Antioxidant additives mixed into the sorbent can slow that decay. They are also easy to add from store-bought materials.

The open question was how humidity changes the chemistry. Livermore ran quantum simulations of oxidation reactions. It predicted the infrared, NMR, and X-ray absorption fingerprints of a library of possible oxidation products, so tests could tell the products apart. Global Thermostat handled synthesis, sample characterization, and decay kinetics. Bond energies tracked oxidation protection only loosely, pointing to steric effects as well. Second-year work turned to naming the products and water's mechanistic role.
doe-osti-3022461-legacy-devices-and-inte:
NLR report NLR/TP-5700-97830, by Andreas Berres and six colleagues, tackles a blind spot in grid research: the old devices still running much of the power system. Transformers, relays, and controls installed 30 to 50 years ago were designed for one-way power flow. Yet studies, testbeds, and standards tend to assume modern equipment. Research results can fail on the grid as it actually exists.

The authors develop a scientific strategy for including legacy devices properly. It covers how to represent them in models and interoperability standards, and how to test modern controls against them. It also addresses keeping rural and remote systems, where old equipment concentrates, from being designed out of the energy transition. The aim is research that respects the installed base instead of wishing it away.
doe-osti-3023346-a-simulator-for-neyer-t:
David H Collins Jr and Michael S Hamada of the Statistical Sciences Group at Los Alamos National Laboratory present a simulator for Neyer tests of explosives, report LA-UR-26-22005, issued March 16, 2026. Neyer tests probe devices such as detonators with rising stimulus levels, voltage or shock, and record a simple binary outcome: detonated or did not detonate. Planners need to know how a test design will perform before spending real devices.

The simulator generates stimulus and response pairs that mimic real tests, with levels rounded to whole values as labs usually do. Fits use a generalized linear model to estimate the mean and standard deviation of the threshold distribution, matching the maximum likelihood estimates from Neyer's Sentest software. Code listings show the function's options, including trace output and saving results to a spreadsheet file.
doe-osti-3023392-high-efficiency-high-cu:
Matthias Fuchs of the University of Nebraska-Lincoln closes award DE-SC0021132, which ran from September 2020 to August 2023 with the BELLA Center at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. His team built and studied a laser-driven electron injector meant to deliver high-current, high-brightness beams efficiently. Laser-plasma acceleration can shrink accelerators greatly, but injection quality decides whether the beams are useful.

Experiments and simulations focused on plasma near quarter-critical density, where stimulated Raman scattering and two-plasmon decay grow strong. The transmitted laser light showed a clear peak near 530 nanometers, the three-halves harmonic of the 800 nanometer drive laser, which signals strong plasma waves at half the laser frequency. The authors read these instabilities as central to how electrons get injected in this regime, with beam results they call unprecedented for gas targets.
doe-osti-3023601-enabling-depth-resolved:
Bram W G Stone, Ryan McClure, Adam Ryan, Vanessa Bailey, and five Pacific Northwest National Laboratory colleagues. They present a new sampler for soil microbes in the vadose zone, the unsaturated ground above the water table, in a March 2026 report. Existing sampling tends to mix depths or freeze one moment in time. Their diffusion sampler is meant to resolve both depth and time at once.

Field deployment used soil stakes with sterile sand and clay inserts placed inside. The plot was irrigated daily with 50 liters of water in total. The first inserts came out on June 17, 2025, after 47 days in the soil, and went on ice, then into storage at minus 20 degrees. A second set followed the same path for 43 days, sampled on July 30, 2025.
doe-osti-3029157-livewire-data-platform-:
Andre Amante and Shuhao Bai of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory lead an eleven-author, three-laboratory team setting file standards for the Livewire Data Platform, version 1.0, dated April 2026. A shared data platform fails quietly when every contributor names files and fields differently. This standard is the house rulebook: dataset contents, file sizes, and naming for raw, processed, and human data.

Field naming rules are exact. A field name starts with a letter, uses uppercase sparingly, joins its parts with underscores, and stays concise; abbreviations are allowed only to shorten overlong names, follow earlier conventions, or add clarity. Private shorthand that only the name's author understands is banned outright. To satisfy the archive database, field names may not exceed 25 characters. The document is versioned at 1.0, a baseline meant to be revised in the open.
doe-osti-3029938-develop-accurate-techni:
Christian M. Petrie, Stephanie Curlin, Annabelle Le Coq, and four colleagues at Oak Ridge National Laboratory refine a thermometer that needs no wires, in report ORNL/TM-2025/4076, dated September 2025. Most fuel and material test capsules carry no live sensors, so staff must infer the heat a sample saw after the test ends. Silicon carbide pieces serve that role: radiation changes them in ways that later lab heating can read back as a peak temperature.

Sharper readings matter for tiny samples used across many test programs, the cross-cutting aim here. The team ran calorimetry scans at set heating rates, such as 10 degrees Celsius per minute with 20 degree cooling. They swapped platinum crucibles for alumina ones after finding silicon carbide reacts with platinum from 1,000 degrees Celsius.
doe-osti-3030106-develop-accurate-techni: SiC monitors got technique-developed again, and this DOE text passively tracks temperature. The pages detail the accurate findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The applications were cross-cutting. The data were nuclear. The again were techniques. The SiC were monitoring.
doe-osti-3363594-metamaterials-as-a-plat:
Willie J. Padilla of Duke University files this final report on metamaterials for energy uses. The grant is DE-SC0014372, from Basic Energy Sciences. The program explored how built structures smaller than a wavelength can control light and energy. It focused on dielectric metasurfaces in the terahertz and infrared. These surfaces offer a low loss path beyond metal designs.

Four thrusts organized the work. They were machine learning for light matter design, zero rank coherent perfect absorbers, bound states in the continuum, and spatial-temporal metasurfaces. Highlights include deep learning that speeds all-dielectric metasurface design. Another is phototunable dielectric Huygens' metasurfaces. The report closes with a long publication list from the award.
doe-osti-3377304-combined-nitrogen-and-p:
Final technical report for award DE-EE0009502, from Ohio University, covers a bid to pull nitrogen and phosphorus out of city wastewater with electrochemical cells. Damilola Daramola led the first budget period; Jason Trembly led the next two. The project ran from September 2021 to August 2025. Partners were Faraday Technology, the cities of Athens and Columbus, and Northeastern University. Plants must strip these nutrients to meet discharge rules. Recovering them as fertilizer turns a cost into a product.
